speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may have the unanimous consent of the house I move, seconded by Mr. Blouin:
That the first report of the standing committee on transport and communications presented to the house on Tuesday, February 22,	1966, be now
concurred in.
That report which was tabled was to allow the committee to sit while the house is sitting to enable representations to be heard from delegations from the Canadian Pacific Railway on a matter referred to that committee by this house on February 8, 1966. We anticipate that we will require this delegation to be here today and tomorrow, and perhaps next week, but I am asking for unanimous consent in regard to today and tomorrow only.

maintopic: TRANSPORT AND COMMUNICATIONS- CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the reasons I gave last week when the adoption of the report of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs was 23033-1331 moved, I objected to the committee sitting when the house is in session. Today the member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso) asks again that the committee sit at the same time as the house. I think this would be nonsense; with the 22 committees we have, if all committee chairmen ask for the same permission, we will never have a sufficient number of members so that the house can sit.
We have a responsibility toward the House of Commons, and that is why I object. If the hon. member wants the committee to sit today and tomorrow, I see no objection to it. On the other hand, if he is trying to get permission to sit next week, I do object, because I feel that is not necessary.
I am told that C.P.R. officials have arrived; I could not care less, and the C.P.R. president can come back; he can spare the time. I would not object, however, if these people were from out of town. Similar requests have been made in the past and I have voiced my objection every time. I am just as much against it today as I was when in opposition. I was very happy to see that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) changed his mind so quickly to support me. If there is not enough time for committees, Wednesday afternoon sittings of the house should be cancelled to allow committees to sit. I have always objected to granting a blanket authorization in this regard, and I am objecting again today.

maintopic: TRANSPORT AND COMMUNICATIONS- CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Hull that the hours of sitting of the committee should not be extended to while the house is sitting, particularly in view of the fact that we are sitting long hours in the house now and I think it would be rather foolish if we divided the strength of the house into committees at the same time.

maintopic: TRANSPORT AND COMMUNICATIONS- CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the same reasons, I object to the committees sitting at the same time as the house. I remember quite well that, during the last election campaign, a minister criticized us for not attending committee sittings, but he forgot to say that committees were sitting
March 3, 1966

Committees of the House at the same time as the house. We were blamed at the time for not attending committee meetings while the house was sitting, and if the same policy is to be followed, steps should be taken to enable members to be present in the house and in the committees. On the other hand, we should not be asked to dislocate ourselves. We are already too few to be required to submit to dislocation and, besides, we do not suffer from that disease.
If the hon. member wants this permission only for today and tomorrow, that is fine with us, but if it is for a longer period, we object and we shall ask for a vote on the matter.

maintopic: TRANSPORT AND COMMUNICATIONS- CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT
speechtext:
So far as
we in this party are concerned we realize that while it may be a strain for some members to attend committee meetings while the house is sitting, at the same time we have to realize that it has been difficult to get all the business done during the session. So far as we are concerned, we are prepared to give consent to some of these committees to sit while the house is sitting because this privilege has not been abused. I believe the only time this permission has been used extensively has been when witnesses have been called to Ottawa from long distances. Certainly we should be able to do that.
However, if there is a great deal of objection to giving blanket permission for the balance of this session, then I would think there probably is a misunderstanding, and perhaps the mover of the motion would agree to have that motion apply to today and tomorrow only. Following that there should be some negotiation between what is called the usual channels to see if we cannot arrive at some agreement with respect to what we are going to do with these motions to allow the committees to meet while the house is sitting.

speechtext: have a question to ask the Secretary of State. Is the minister in a position to reply today to the question which her parliamentary secretary took as notice a few days ago, in relation to the dispute between the C.B.C. and some of its employees? I asked whether the minister could make a full statement with regard to the strike which is being proposed by the writers and performers.

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Secretary of Stale):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: REPORTED STRIKE DEADLINE BY WRITERS AND PERFORMERS
speechtext:
I have been in touch with the president of the C.B.C. on this subject and can report the following to the house.
As has been reported, the president of the C.B.C. has wired Mr. Comor of ACTRA offering to meet with him informally tomorrow to explain the reasons behind corporation policy in regard to increased work opportunities for Canadian talent. Mr. Ouimet informs me that he is meeting Mr. Comor for lunch tomorrow.
Mr. Comor has, at the same time, sent a telegram to the Prime Minister requesting a meeting with various members of the government to discuss the situation. Consideration is now being given by the government to this request.
As to the issues in dispute, I think the house should note there is no disagreement over the basic principle involved, namely that increased work opportunities should be provided by the corporation for Canadian writers and artists. The corporation's agreement with this principle has been stated several times both by its board and its chief executive officers, and was implemented in the C.B.C.'s announcement of February 23 that it has committed an additional $850,000 of its 1966-67 operating budget to provide increased work opportunities for ACTRA members. This represents a very substantial increase, about 20 per cent, in funds committed to this specific purpose.
The point currently at issue is whether this public commitment should be formally written into the union contract as a work guarantee. The corporation, for its part, has taken the position that such a procedure would be
March 3. 1966

unacceptable in that it would limit essential program flexibility. The result of such a step, in the C.B.C.'s view, would be of real benefit neither to its performers nor to the listening and viewing public.
Mr. Speaker, that in brief is the current situation, I am informed.

maintopic: REPORTED STRIKE DEADLINE BY WRITERS AND PERFORMERS
speechtext: On a point of order, I respectfully submit that the Secretary of State has done an injustice to the bargaining procedure by making a statement in this house which sets out the reasons why the employer refuses to put something into a collective agreement, without at the same time telling us the reasons why ACTRA want it put into the agreement. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want first of all to thank members of the committee for having permitted us to proceed in this way. I am quite certain that all of us regret very much that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys has been called away today. The Minister without Portfolio and myself will do our best to deal with the estimates and endeavour to answer all the questions put to us.
The only preliminary statement I would make, and it will be very short, is that I

2108	COMMONS DEBATES	March 3. 1966
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys think there is general agreement in the house, and certainly I feel there is in the country, that there is a great advantage in bringing together under one department the consideration and administration of the resources of Canada so far as they come within the federal responsibility.
We are a resource rich nation and I would remind my hon. friend from Kamloops, who knows this as well as I, that in the field of resources those resources which lie within each separate province are jealously guarded by the province concerned. After all, the resources that lie there are their main sources of revenue; they are the main means by which they can develop industry and enhance the economy within their own provincial boundaries. It would be unusual, indeed I think we would agree that the provinces would not be doing their duty if this were not the case, if they did not keep a jealous eye on their resources.
However, from a national point of view we must recall that the resources of Canada were not shared equitably when they were placed by divine Providence. We must remember too that there are tremendous advantages in using these resources as broadly as we possibly can and living off of them within Canada without importing by extending the products of resources, for example, power, to more than one province. Therefore there is a very great place for a national policy, national incentives and national leadership.
That being the case, Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister decided in co-operation and consultation with the ministry to put the resources of Canada in their national context under one minister. I wish to compliment that particular minister because he has been placed in charge of a most interesting department dealing with falling water, electrical energy, thermal energy, atomic energy, the possibility of having strings of wire across this country serving more than one province and the study of the rivers of Canada. Again, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Kamloops and I are very conscious of those values to the provinces themselves since we come from British Columbia where we think we have a potential in excess of 30 million kilowatts of falling water electrical energy alone. We have in recent years gone a very great way forward in supporting the provinces in these fields and I am quite certain that with the new dispensation in respect of the department we shall move forward very quickly indeed.

I think there is general agreement within the house that the new minister is young, energetic and extremely able. I believe he will develop this department very well indeed and to the great credit of Canada. What we want to do, in all these matters, without invading the rights of any province, is to bring together the collective advantages of the resources that lie within the provinces and utilize them in such a way in a national sense that, hopefully, they will mean more than a simple addition to the resources within the various provinces. That is our objective, of course.
I wish to pay a compliment now, as I have before, to the work of one of my predecessors who in 1961 convened the resources conference in Montreal. I have said, and I say again, that I wish this great report were required reading for every Canadian because there is contained in it a tremendous amount of valuable information concerning all Canadian resources.
I hope the new minister will redouble the efforts we have made in recent years to bring together the resource ministers of the 10 provinces and keep in constant touch with them in order to get their co-operation, add together the collective resources of the individual provinces and by a national and purposeful policy make them more valuable than they are today.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for having made this statement although I would wish it might have been somewhat more enlightening as to the bases upon which this policy is to rest. I think this would have been helpful in that we do not wish to prolong debate at this stage for a variety of reasons but we would like to have had a statement on the position of the government. Such a statement could have been considered in the meantime and would have served as a starting point in considering the estimates of the year 1966-67 when they come before us.
In light of the fact that we are prepared to extend our co-operation with respect to expediting the passage of these estimates, I think we might well have been favoured with a somewhat more detailed statement of the position.
However, perhaps we can leave it on the basis that during the course of what I have to say I will serve notice as to areas which we feel are of greatest concern and which we will discuss when the new estimates are before us. At that time we shall expect the
March 3, 1966

fullest information. We take this position because we do not feel we should take very long in the discussion of these estimates. After all, although we have a new minister these are the old estimates for the year 196566. Eleven-twelfths of them have now been spent. We intend therefore to leave the main discussion for the 1966-67 estimates, at which time I think the new minister, to whom we extend the best of personal good wishes as he undertakes these very important responsibilities, will perhaps be more fairly expected to be thoroughly conversant with the matters about which he will be questioned.
But we are dealing here with what is one of the most important fields included within the area of government responsibility. We therefore do not intend just to pass this subject by without stating some of the considerations which we think should apply in developing policy in this field. After all, Mr. Chairman, the field of resource policy, which embraces the whole complex and vital area of water use, the area of energy development, distribution and marketing, the area of mines and minerals development and the policy regarding the disposition of the products of the mine-all this comprises a policy field which to no country is more vital than to Canada.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
For it is true that in this area there lies the potential for Canada's future greatness. It is also an important and basic truth that in wise policies and only in wise policies for the development and conservation of our resources in these areas lies the answer to the question of whether we shall have a Canadian identity and continue in the future to exercise control of our own affairs. In the existence or in the absence of such wise policies lies the answer to the question of whether or not we slide down the slope called continentalism into the extinction of anything which might be called nationhood on the basis of which we could have a separate Canadian identity.
This is the vital question, the solution to which I feel lies in the fields we are discussing today, the fields of energy, mines and resource development and the development of policies which should govern those fields. We will naturally be expected to watch the government and to watch the new minister with the greatest interest, and we are entitled to expect from the new minister and the government an early and full declaration of the policies and the principles which will guide
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys the new department which has the opportunity to play such a fundamental role in the future of Canada. We shall then serve notice now as to some of the areas about which we will expect full discussion and action by the time the estimates for 1966-67 are before us. I should also like to lay down on behalf of the Conservative party some of the principles that we feel should guide the development of policy in this field.
We feel, first, there should be the earliest possible assessment of Canada's full potential in terms of resources and of Canada's full potential requirements for those resources. After all, a knowledge of your inventory and a knowledge of your needs is the cornerstone of any sound policy. We hope, therefore, to receive assurances that there will be, by means of the conference of resource ministers and other agencies, the earliest and most aggressive pursuit, in co-operation with the provinces, of the completion of the inventory of Canada's storehouse and of the inventory of Canada's present and future requirements.
Second, we urge upon the government that all policy and action in this field be based upon the general principle of conservation to meet Canada's known and potential requirements. There should be a statement of the perimeters of these requirements and of this principle as the basis upon which all Canadian policy will be founded, and without it there should be no negotiation or consideration of negotiation for the disposition of these resources beyond our borders.
Third, and equally important, of course, as a cornerstone of policy in this field, is the necessity of the utmost co-operation with the provincial governments in every aspect of resource development policy. This has been alluded to by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and I confirm my complete agreement with him in his statement of that position. I think it is important not just to say we intend to co-operate but that we should avoid taking any position in this area, especially publicly, which appears to involve a statement of federal policy and objectives in an area which lies within provincial jurisdiction before the matter has been discussed fully with the provinces. 1 think it is not unnatural that the provinces are expressing concern about these matters and about the future of confederation when they find that so frequently the federal government is stating publicly its objectives and its positions on matters which are also of provincial concern, without such discussion. Now I can well understand the conflict which has been going on here and I can well understand the position of my hon. friend who is a minister from British Columbia. But it is illogical in the extreme-"illogical" is a mild word; a far stronger word would do-to allow personal considerations to govern the sound administration and sound outline of government policy.
In fact it is farcical, and I do not hesitate to use that word, to set up a department with a great fanfare and to say: We are now going to co-ordinate policy in the field of resource development, and then to carve out of it one of the most substantial and important areas, if not the most important area, in the field of federal responsibility, leaving the minister responsible for resource policy co-ordination and development with only part of the jurisdiction.
Compare what is happening, Mr. Chairman, with the expectations aroused by the Prime Minister when he was discussing the setting up of this department. I should like to refer to a report in the Toronto Star, which I do not think could be considered unfair to the

A department of resources and energy.
The aim here is to bring all energy and resources affairs under one cabinet roof.
Certainly that is a logical and proper objective. The article continues:
At present they're scattered among a number of departments and ministers.

It does my heart good to see us co-operating in this respect. I know other hon. members want to make a few remarks-

The hon. gentleman need not reassess his position. He will be following a good lead. Like the hon. member, I should have liked to hear the minister give more information as to the government's purposes and objectives with respect to a national water policy. I realize the difficulties. The government must recognize the responsibilities of the provinces. There will be conferences and discussions and a water policy is not going to be devised overnight. I should like to have the minister tell the house what the government's purpose is and what its objectives are so far as the future is concerned. Like the hon. member for Kamloops-I am quite sure hon. members have heard me say this on a number of previous occasions-we believe that there is a necessity for an inventory of our water resources in Canada and an inventory of our needs for this generation and for some generations to come.
I want once again to pay tribute to General Andrew McNaughton who recently brought this matter to the attention of the Canadian people through an address to the Engineering Institute of Canada and, I think, to the Canadian Club in Montreal during the election. I notice that various candidates discussed the questions he raised more fully after his address. In that connection may I draw the attention of hon. members to an article written by Mr. Walter Stewart, found in the Star Weekly magazine of February 26, 1966. I want to quote briefly from the article because I think it says very succinctly what the hon. members for Kamloops and Kootenay West wish to say in this regard:
We were "skinned alive".
"With the knowledge that water is going up in value 10 or 15 per cent a year . . . the average over the 30 years (the first stage of the treaty) can certainly be taken at $10 an acre foot. To show you that's not unreasonable, the value of water today in a citrus field is about $70 an acre foot. So 15.5 million acre feet made available is $155 million a year-

The reference to $70 an acre foot is in the United States.

The value for power purposes was put at $501 million for 30 years, whereas if you take $155 million a year as the figure, even allowing the Americans a good discount because they are paying in advance, you'll find it works out to $2.65 billion over the 30 years.
"In other words, the consumptive uses of the water, which are not provided for in any way in the treaty, are worth five times more than the power benefits paid Canada."
I am glad to see that the house is not divided on this occasion and that the majority of the members here are not going to let this happen again so far as the disposal of our water resources is concerned.
Recently I had occasion to attend the annual meeting of the Royal Geographical Society. Professor Trevor Lloyd was the guest speaker. He gave what I thought was a most interesting address. I wish to quote briefly from it because he concluded by in effect supporting the approach taken by General McNaughton, an attitude which has been adopted by numerous other engineers in this country. His address is reported in the Globe and Mail of Friday, February 25, in an article headed "Scheme To Divert Canadian Water Assailed". The article reads:
A leading Canadian geographer last night described a scheme to divert Canadian water to the United States as "an exercise in sophomore civil engineering"-
He described the NAWAPA scheme in these terms:
"Water from the Canadian cordillera will be turned south to meet the supposed needs of the United States Southwest. Anything which survives after passing Southern California will go on to the arid areas of Mexico.
An incidental but unavoidable result of the scheme would be to drown out most of the usable level land in interior British Columbia.
The water needs of Canada are not overlooked. The Prairies will be allocated at least as much of the water as will Mexico."
He took note of plans under the scheme for a seaway to James Bay, "where, as is well known, the offshore waters are so shallow that even a canoe cannot be assured of getting within sight of land at low tide."
Prof. Lloyd called for the formulation of a national water policy for Canada, but placed consideration of diversion to the United States last in his list of seven policy requirements.
He noted he had "ventured outside the usual academic pale to comment on public policy. It is apparent that water has now become a subject of major concern within Canada and that it will influence relations between this country and the United States in the years ahead."

I may say that I agree with him in this respect and so do other members of this group. The article continues:
"It does not appear, for example, to have worked smoothly in relation to utilization of the Columbia River water. The suggestion has been made that, in a strictly technical sense, Canada has not always been sufficiently skilful to maintain its authority in the partnership."
He cited water demands in California as an example of increasing pressure on Canada by the United States and quoted the governor of California, Edmund Brown, as saying: "Whether we bring it from the Snake, the Columbia or the Volga, we will have to have it."
I place this on the record because I am in the habit of sending out copies of Hansard to a number of people in my constituency and this is a cheap way of letting them know what Professor Lloyd had to say on this occasion.
I turn now to another aspect of this matter. It appears there has been considerable trouble over the construction of the High Arrow Dam. In fairness to some people who are closely connected with this job, I cannot say much about what they have told me. To be quite safe I will quote from the Nelson Daily News of February 24, 1966. Under a headline "Error Delays Arrow Dam Project" we find the following:
Vancouver sources reported Wednesday that the construction schedule at the dam has been hard hit by inaccuracies in engineering data supplied to the dam builders. Core drillings reportedly showing solid bed rock proved false when the underlying structures were found to be weakened by dirt seams and cracks.
The project is really in much greater difficulty than would appear from this article. I think this proves that General McNaughton's scepticism before the committee was well justified. Then the article goes on to say:
Nearly 10,000 extra cubic yards of rock will have to be removed from the north end of the dam site. Misinformation will cause an added three weeks work to be crammed into an already rigid schedule, the sources said.
The article continues:
The north end is not the only unknown factor. A centre section of the concrete half, running about 300 feet along its baseline is as yet unexplored. Rather than waste time by drilling, crews are blasting the surface of this area off in layers to reach solid ground.
The article then goes on to deal with other difficulties which are being experienced. I mention this because of General McNaughton's expressed concern about the foundations of this dam when he was giving evidence before the External Affairs Committee.

Hydro. I trust the minister will agree to tabling this report for our information.
I have referred to these few matters briefly. I realize there is a long road to travel before we can finally have a national water policy. As I say, I wish the minister would inform the house more fully as to the government's purpose and objectives in this respect after it has had an opportunity to discuss these matters with the provinces particularly concerned.
I have always been interested in keeping our water clean and free from pollution. It is a serious question and one of growing concern in the area I have the honour to represent. There is pollution in the upper Columbia. There is pollution in Kootenay Lake. There is some pollution in the lower Columbia before it enters the United States. This situation has caused alarm to rod and gun clubs, chambers of commerce and labour organizations who believe we can only deal effectively with pollution of rivers of this type when we have a national policy which will provide for co-operation between federal, provincial and municipal governments.

Mr. Chairman, we are now studying the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. The people I represent are very much interested in mining development and the development of new mining industries in Northwestern Quebec.
I note, in the estimates of the department, that an amount of $16 million is allotted to help the gold mines in Canada. I have not made a break-down of the subsidies granted each mine, but we have a table of these figures.
I feel the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys should give far more attention to gold mines than it does at the present time.
Here is what I read in the report on the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act:
The annual average of the weekly buying prices in Canadian funds at the Royal Canadian Mint in 1964 was $37.75 per fine ounce of gold. This compares with $37.75 in 1963 and $37.41 in 1962. The price of gold in Canadian funds is governed by the fixed buying price of $35 per fine ounce in United States funds by the United States Treasury and the exchange rate between the Canadian and United States dollars. Since May 2, 1962 the value of the Canadian dollar has been set at $0,925 United States funds. At parity, the Mint buying price for gold is $37.84 per ounce in Canadian funds. The market value of the Canadian dollar may be permitted to fluctuate by 1 per cent either side of parity. Thus, the Mint buying price in Canadian funds may vary between $37.46 and $38.22 per ounce. In 1964, the Mint price varied from $37.54 to $37.86 per ounce.
When the government starts helping the gold mines or granting subsidies to the gold mines:
The average cost of production per ounce of gold, computed on all ounces of gold produced from the mine during the designated period, must exceed $26.50.
-and not more than $45.
It means that the government helps between $26.50 and $45, for a total of $12.33 per ounce, which is the maximum rate paid to gold producers in Canada.
On page 9 of that blue booklet, one can read:
The Gold Export Act and Disposal of Canadian Gold
The Gold Export Act, passed in 1932, authorized the Governor in Council to make regulations regarding the export of gold from Canada. On March 21, 1956, the regulations, which prohibited the export in any form except under licence issued by the Minister of Finance, were revoked. Thus, since March 1956, producers have been free to sell their gold wherever they wish.

Mr. Chairman, I think that practice is not followed at all although it would be practicable since there are countries which would pay more than $35 or $37 per ounce for gold produced in Canada.
But here is the problem with regard to assistance to gold mining. In my region, and the other gold producing regions, the employees, those who work in a gold mine are paid $1 or $1.50 in some cases, less than those who work in other mines such as copper, nickel, zinc, etc.
In gold mines, we still have people working at an hourly rate of $1.40 or $1.45, and subsidies are paid to mines to keep them in operation.
I see no objection to that, sir, and I would even urge the government to give more subsidies so that a greater number of gold mines remain in operation, but those supplementary subsidies should be subject to the provision that the wages of miners working in those mines are to be adjusted so that their standard of living is as good and as high as that of miners working in other mining enterprises.
I believe that is a very serious shortcoming that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys should correct as soon as possible. We have been asking for several years to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to consider the question-not on the surface but in depth-in short to consider the situation as it is.
A few months ago, I attended the official opening of a new gold mine in our region, the Wasamak mine located about six or seven miles from Rouyn-Noranda, and the owners of that mine make applications to, and apply the pressure on the government in order to derive profits from their operations.
Those who provide capital and equipment for the operation of a mine want to make a profit, and you cannot blame them. In my region, a number of mines only make a profit because of the grants received from the federal Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. They cannot, of course, raise miners' salaries so that the men would make a decent living, and that is the problem.
A miner working eight hours a day, either underground or in the plant, is putting in a hard day's work. He has a rather serious responsibility and must often work under dangerous conditions.


Therefore, I urge the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Pepin) to study the question of gold mines in our region and to consider the possibility of helping them or of suggesting to other departments, the Department of Industry for instance, the establishment in our region of secondary industries to process the ores, either for the domestic or the export trade.
But one point on which I want to insist is that adequate subsidies be paid to the producing gold mines in our region to enable their owners to grant salary increases to the miners who could then give their families better living conditions. It is not that they do not want to but they are unable to do so because of the economic conditions resulting from this niggardliness on the part of the government which will not give more help for the operation of gold mines in our region.
When I think that Canada is giving millions of dollars to other countries to help underdeveloped and needy people, when I hear the ministers, one after the other, talk about fighting poverty and misery in Canada, I say that the gold mine employees are now the victims of that poverty and that it is the responsibility of the government to help them by increasing subsidies for gold production. Not to increase the wealth of company presidents, but to enable the companies to pay their employees higher, more adequate salaries, taking into account the present needs in our area and in all similar regions.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to pursue the subject, but I strongly urge the minister concerned to study thoroughly and in detail this matter of gold mines and the industries which could be established in our region, so as to help increase Canadian production including that of our province.
I strongly urge that the problem arising in my region be considered and that the different cases be studied and dealt with, not by means of political partisanship, but effectively, so that our people may receive fair and equitable treatment.

Mr. Chairman, because of our concern for the Nova Scotia coal industry and our greater concern for the number of miners and their families involved in this industry, it is most important that we impress upon the government today the need for assistance. I regret very much that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys is not available today and that we have to put our case to two ministers
March 3, 1966

who are quite far removed from the problem, although we do have present the Minister of National Health and Welfare, not because of his own initiative, I might say, but because of an arrangement made by his house leader.
Since the house opened we have been denied on any number of occasions the opportunity of pinpointing this particular problem. The Minister of National Health and Welfare gleefully hides behind a ruling of the Chair to the effect that we can no longer ask questions of ministers on the basis of the province from which they come but only questions which refer immediately to their departments. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has been able to hide behind that ruling which has been invoked during this session but which was never before applicable.
I hope it will be possible before the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys are passed to hear some answers from the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In the meantime I hope the Minister without Portfolio and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will listen to the arguments put forward today and realize that the government has to take immediate action in order to salvage and save the Nova Scotia coal industry.
I should like to thank the hon. member for Kamloops for making reference to the fact that I would have something to say regarding the Dominion Coal Board. However, I intend to range a little wider than that. In thanking him I am reminded that this was not his only concern or the only concern of the government of which he was a member. The former Conservative government took every possible step to assist the Nova Scotia coal industry and met every demand made by that industry. In fact, on one occasion, in order to extend the life of a colliery that was to be closed, the government of that day offered assistance but the company did not see fit to accept it with the result that we lost one coal mine.
The importance and urgency of this matter are with us every day. We have had another mine closure and we are now expecting to have a mine opening. I should like to take exception to what the hon. member for Kamloops referred to as a political promise made during the election campaign. I want the government and the three ministers now present to understand that it was not a political promise. In that regard I can quote

In order to emphasize this matter I state here and now that the minister and his colleagues in Nova Scotia relied heavily on this $25 million commitment to the Cape Breton coal industry to get elected. Again I emphasize the fact that the Minister of National Health and Welfare said this was not a political promise or a part of the Liberal party's platform but was a definite commitment on the part of the government.
To back up the fact that this was a commitment I should like to quote from the instruction that every Liberal poll worker in Cape Breton South had. This instruction reads:
The Liberal Government and Allan MacEachen got 25 million dollars for the coal industry. No matter how you voted in the past Liberals should have your vote this one time. The Liberal is Joe MacEachern. Voters should be shown the sample ballot In this book.
Again I say to the minister that I have every indication that a number of Liberal workers who are more concerned about the coal industry in Nova Scotia than they are about the Liberal Party are prepared to sign an affidavit to the effect that this was the instruction they were given on election day.

I might say at this point that since this announcement was made the government has been hiding behind what they refer to as the Dr. Donald report which had nothing to do with the $25 million. In this regard I can quote the words of the Minister of National Health and Welfare who, when speaking of the $25 million in aid, spoke of it as being an accomplished fact. I will remind the minister of his own words and indicate where and when he said them. It is imperative that we get this money and get that mine operating within the time limit mentioned by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The article to which I referred states:
The federal government will dip into the treasury for at least 25 million in a long range gamble to shore up Cape Breton's erratic coal industry.
Labour Minister Allan MacEachen held court at b press conference in Halifax Tuesday and in less than 500 words spelled out a formula that could herald a new era for coal.
Mr. MacEachen said the government was prepared to "invest" at least 25 million dollars in -Cape Breton coal mining future including the first major mine opening in more than two decades in the Province.
"Good news." "Fantastic." More than we had hoped for from the federal government was the immediate comment from District 26 President, Bill Marsh who sat beside Mr. MacEachen for the official announcement. Dominion Coal Company President Earl Clubb checked in fast with similar words of praise.
"This announcement will be received with enthusiasm by the people of Cape Breton", Mr. Clubb said. "This will do much to stabilize the industry."
Mr. MacEachen said that 10 million dollars would be spent to open a mine at Lingan and another 15 million allotted to rehabilitate and automate the coal mines now operating.
It was Allan MacEachen's stature in the cabinet that was the turning point in the long negotiations.

$25 Million Boost for Coal!
Pit for Lingan
It was a day of good news-multimillion dollar news-yesterday for the ailing Nova Scotia coal industry.
In Halifax Labour Minister Allan MacEachen announced that about $25 million in federal funds would be invested in the coal industry to provide for a new mine at Lingan and to modernize production machinery at other mines.
An estimated $25 million funds will be poured into the Cape Breton coal industry to provide for the capital investment of opening a new mine at Lingan and modernizing production machinery in other mines in the area, Labour Minister Allan J. MacEachen announced yesterday.

Reference was made also to the fact that this new mine opening could be used to tap both the harbour seam and the Phalen seam and that plans to do just that have gone ahead. The only thing that is holding them up is the $25 million which, according to the former minister of labour and the former minister of mines and technical surveys, was all but delivered to Cape Breton. Yet they hide behind Dr. Donald and his report.
I inquired about Dr. Donald only last week from officials of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the U.M.W. executive. I asked whether Dr. Donald had visited Cape Breton and gone underground. To their knowledge he had not. Nobody could say he had and nobody could say he had not, but

nobody could support the idea that he had gone underground.
What is Dr. Donald going to do? My understanding of Dr. Donald-I am not criticizing him because I have no idea what the man's particular job is and I am waiting with interest the results of his report-is that he is an engineer in the chemicals field. The name of the former minister of mines and technical surveys was mentioned and I will get tc him a little later. I might also say that the former minister of labour took great exception to the remarks made. He happened to get bumped down to National Health and Welfare but nevertheless he is still representing Nova Scotia and should take the opportunity under our practice to enlighten the people of Nova Scotia in respect of his commitments prior to the election, what his intentions are now and whether he will meet with the same success with his cabinet colleagues. Here I quote the minister himself:
And just last week I had the great privilege, and it was a privilege because I had worked hard to bring it about-
I am sure the Minister of National Health and Welfare will not take objection to these words. They are his own and I will repeat them:
And just last week I had the great privilege, and it was a privilege because I had worked hard to bring it about, to announce the new plans of the federal government for the coal industry, bringing relief and a sense of particular joy to the coal miners and their families living in so many communities in this part of Nova Scotia; a plan that will modernize and re-equip the existing industry; a plan that will make it possible to open a new mine, something that has been sought and asked for, something that has now been done by a federal Liberal government at Ottawa.
I emphasize the minister's own words:
-something that has now been done by a federal Liberal government at Ottawa. This is quite a story of achievement, in my view, for the people of Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia. It has been done by a government that is deeply interested in developing all parts of Canada.
I can say, I am sure with absolute certainty, that no government in the history of this country has done as much for the island of Cape Breton and eastern Nova Scotia than this present government at Ottawa in 30 months of its life.

Mr. Marsh is quite right. This policy represents a major breakthrough for our economy, for the miners, their wives and families. No other government in Canada's history has demonstrated such willingness to support and maintain the coal industry of Cape Breton.
I am sorry that Premier Stanfield and his followers have failed to appreciate the significance of this tremendous undertaking.
I interrupt at this point to emphasize the fact that this was not a political promise, it was not a campaign promise and it was not part of their platform, but boy did they use it.

Now, it has a chance to survive and, we hope, to prosper. I also stated on October 5 that a comprehensive long term procram for the coal industry would be introduced in 1966.

I am not sufficiently familiar with the members of the Dominion Coal Board to know how many of them are competent to take this position. However, I know from experience that there must be many men in the employment of the board who could do a very good job. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in 1957 when the Canadian Pacific switched over from the use of coal burning engines to diesel engines there was a tremendous amount of unemployment and distress in the Crowsnest Pass area. Many of the people were at their wits' end to know what they were going to do. Some people moved out. However, the shipments of coal to Japan, the winter works program and other things gave some employment to the people who remained in the area and enabled them to remain in the area until times got better.
The subvention which was first paid on these coal shipments was around $4.25 per ton whereas today it is $2.73. The cost of transporting coal from the Crowsnest Pass to Port Moresby jumped from $5.13 per ton to $5.28 per ton, another 15 cents. This brings me to the point I want to bring to the attention of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. At the time these coal shipments to Japan were arranged our understanding was that after these shipments had reached a certain volume there would be a reconsideration of the question of subventions. I may say that these shipments have reached approximately 800,000 tons, which amounts to a considerable business. The present government went along with the program and paid the subsidy on another 200,000 tons, bringing it up to around 800,000 tons.

March 3, 1966

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys This action by the present government gives me a lot of satisfaction because I was the originator of the coal shipments to Japan. I fought like a tiger to bring them into being and to make sure that economically it was a sound development.
As a matter of fact, everyone in the coal business of the West is solidly behind this development. Where are we now? We want the Canadian Pacific Railway to cut the cost of transporting the coal from the Crowsnest Pass to Port Moresby. As I have said, they are charging $5.28 per ton. Our intention was, if we could get volume shipments, to have the Canadian Pacific cut their cost a little bit, that the operators would perhaps take a little less profit, the handling charges at Port Moresby could be lowered a little bit and we could get the Japanese to pay a little bit more and thus do away with the $2.73 subvention. These shipments are made for the most part in Japanese bottoms.
That was our intention at the beginning. Today, after some six or eight years, we have reached the position where the operators are within sight of accomplishing that end and we could increase the shipments of coal to two million or three million tons. The Japanese want the coal. Lord knows, we have enough coal of that type to last us for 2,000 years. We need not feel that we are digging into something we are going to need tomorrow.
Our sales of coal to Japan are going to help the economy of western Canada and help employment in the industry. The Crowsnest Pass area is going to boom. It is going to help Canada's exports. This is an economic development of great value to Canada. I hope that the log jam which is now preventing that development from taking place can be removed. What is the log jam? It is the fact that the Canadian Pacific, instead of lowering their rates, increased them by 15 cents a ton in October during the last election campaign. The rate is now $5.28. If the Canadian Pacific would give us a commuter train from Coleman to Port Moresby, a quick turnaround train such as they have in the United States, we would be able to cut the cost of transporting the coal by $1.50 per ton. If this is done I believe that the $2.73, by taking a chip off here and a chip off there, could be eliminated and the operators could obtain contracts with Japan for increased coal shipments amounting to two million or three million tons.


[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
That is where we stand on the shipment of coal to Japan and on the whole problem of exporting coal from western Canada. May I summarize what I have said by asking two or three questions? First, I wonder whether the minister is familiar with the problem? If he is not, let him go out west and find out. This is what we want. We do not want any more fooling around with this thing. We have been talking to him gently in the hope he would see the light and be interested enough in western Canada to go out and familiarize himself with the problem and develop an action program in co-operation with the people out west. Then we want to have a discussion with the Canadian Pacific to get this idea across. How active have the minister and his associate been in helping to arrange the C.P.R. commuter train desired by all associated with the industry? What attitude does the C.P.R. take with respect to commencing a commuter train service, cutting costs and bringing about this entire development?
These are questions to which I hope the new minister will provide answers, Mr. Chairman. I shall reserve any further discussion until the estimates for the coming year are before us for debate during the course of the next few weeks.

Jean-Luc Pepin, federal minister of mines and technical surveys, said Tuesday that if bilingualism and biculturalism do not become realities soon "I will resign."
If he does not act in the manner we expect him to act in regard to the coal mining industry and show as much interest as we in Nova Scotia and the coal mining areas in Canada expect from him, then I suggest that he should resign. If he wants to make marks for himself in the coal mining areas, all he has to do is to indicate how soon something will be done about the announcement by the former minister of labour, now Minister of National Health and Welfare, which was made on October 5. I do not know why the statement was made at that time, although there was an election on November 8. I hope he will do everything he can.
I was going to invite him today to visit the coal mining areas. The Minister of National
Health and Welfare said the new minister was planning to do this. I think it is an excellent idea to go to the scene and to see at first hand what a mine looks like. Perhaps the minister has been down coal mines before. I do not know, but I think it is a very good idea and I commend it to the minister. He will receive a very warm welcome, I am sure, in Cape Breton, provided that he attends a press conference there and spells out in detail just what the $25 million which supposedly has been appropriated for assistance to coal mines is going to do.
At this time I should also like to pay tribute to the retiring chairman of the Dominion Coal Board, Mr. C. L. O'Brian, who is rounding out, I understand, 40 years in the civil service. He is a man who has been most capable and still is. He very graciously stayed on in his position at the request of the previous government and the present government. He is a man who came to the old fuel board, as it was known, in 1935 and became chairman of the Dominion Coal Board in 1961. He will certainly be a great loss to the coal industry, though I hope he will not be leaving the public service entirely. I would suggest that the government retain Mr. O'Brian in an advisory capacity because his services are certainly going to be needed.
Some mention has been made of the new coal board chairman. I am not going into that other than to say that I am firmly convinced that the new chairman is going into a field for which he has no background whatever. Contrary to what has been suggested by the Minister of National Health and Welfare concerning an appointment as chairman of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission made by the previous administration, the former member for Inverness-Richmond was well qualified for a position of that nature. He was a professional man and has certainly made his mark as chairman of that board.
I should also like to pay tribute to members of the house who are with us no longer, the late Hon. George Nowlan and the late Hon. Paul Comtois. Mr. Nowlan and Mr. Comtois worked very well together. Mr. Comtois was minister of mines and did a very good job. Did the hon. member wish to interject?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to pose several questions to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and ask him this question.
Regardless of what the Donald report says, is it the intention of the government to go ahead with this $25 million grant? Would the minister tell me also that it is not the intention of the government in the foreseeable future to agree that there shall be a cut-back in the work force of the coal mining industry as suggested in an issue of the Financial Times, I think it was? Mr. Chairman, I was very interested in hearing this afternoon a discussion between representatives of one section of

Canada and their minister. I wanted to ask whether that minister believes he has authority to speak on behalf of the Department of Mines and Technicial Surveys and make this promise of $25 million. If there are possibilities of this kind we in other parts of the country are interested in adopting the minister for ourselves.
I noticed that the hon. gentleman was willing to defend a new appointment to the coal board and he made a number of statements about appointments and patronage such as goes on in the maritimes. It seems to be a fairly open subject in that part of the country. I am not saying it is bad but if there is a constitutional basis for this kind of representation I should like to know what it is because some of the rest of us would like to have it. I am sure hon. members from British Columbia would find a minister of this kind very valuable if he were willing to make the same kind of commitment as that which has been made with respect to the Maritimes.
I was also interested in the remarks made by hon. members with regard to the coal situation in the Maritimes. There is no coal in my area or in northern Ontario generally but there is a great similarity between the problems there and the problems which face the Maritimes. We are dependant on natural resources and on the mining industry for much of our wealth and we are now facing a situation which people in the maritimes have been facing for a long time, the closing of mines which are coming to the end of their operation. We do not seem to be doing anything about it.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
We are not particular about having promises such as they seem to have had in the Maritimes; they certainly seem to have had a whole lot of them. There have been many promises of a political nature in the Maritimes in the last two years in respect of what was going to be done. I think the problem in the Maritimes is one which has to be solved, because when a solution is found it probably will apply also to the mining industry in northern Ontario.
I am interested in another field today. I am well aware of the fact that the two ministers here probably are more competent in the field of water resources, since I have had some experience with them in a committee on this subject. I should like to go into the matter of the diversion of water from James Bay and
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys Hudson Bay into the waters of the Great Lakes chain, because I am sure we probably would get more answers in this regard than in some other fields. However, I think the other fields probably are more important to the people whom I represent.
I will be a little like the hon. member from the Maritimes and will speak mainly of an area in northern Ontario which has problems very similar to the problems to which the hon. member from the Maritimes referred. I am referring to the area encompassing Sudbury, Timmins, Timiskaming, Cochrane and several ridings on the Quebec side of the border. One of the problems we have is in relation to the gold mining industry. If there ever was anything closely connected with government, it certainly is the gold mining industry because of the manipulations which have been carried on by governments not only in Canada but throughout the world with regard to this very important commodity, gold.
I am not particularly sure that we should go back to the gold standard but I am of the opinion that the Canadian government must give consideration to what they really want to accomplish in respect of gold and other precious metals and the relation these have to our international trade, the international monetary fund and, yes, the gold of the Canadian nation. We allow gold to be sold at a fixed price in the United States when there are markets across the world which will pay two or three times the amount of money that the United States is prepared to pay.
Our whole gold system in Canada is in chaos. We, as are other countries, are faced with the fight that is taking place in respect of the backing of currency by gold or by the United States dollar. I think it would have been interesting if Mr. de Gaulle had been a few years younger and had had a few more dollars in bullion under the bed to recall in gold the money lent by the United States to France and then decide whether the backing for United States dollars should be by the International Monetary Fund or whether gold should be the commodity.
It is interesting, when speaking about the role of gold in currency, to point out that when the United States was in serious difficulty in the early 1930's President Roosevelt raised the price of gold from $28 to $35 and at the same time put in a clause to the effect that under the same Act gold could be raised to $50. It is also interesting to note that when

2138	COMMONS
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys the Republicans at a later date decided to raise it to $50 they found there was a clause there which meant that the whole matter had to be reviewed again in the manner which President Roosevelt had followed and the government of the day did not decide to do this.
I think the Canadian people should consider gold as another commodity. We should either keep it in Canada and decide for ourselves what the commodity should be worth -I presume we could sell it internationally at $70 an ounce-or we should decide to keep it in Canada in the reserves of the nation so that we too could deal with the United States in terms of currency and leave the gold in storage in Canada until something is done about it internationally.
It is fair to say that this government has no intention of increasing the price of gold; it is also a fact that the previous government had no intention of increasing the price of gold. I think it will be some time before a minister of finance from Canada will go to the international monetary fund with a few of his colleagues and ask for an increase in the price of gold, even with the support of some of the other nations who are going to ask for it.
I think we should be prepared in Canada to decide for ourselves the price of gold and to allow such prices for that commodity in the gold mining industry which would expand that industry so that it can pay wages and operate the mines. This would result in a great increase in the production of gold and in the development of many areas in Canada. If we do not intend to do this, then let us close down the gold mines and do something for the people of those communities and not keep dragging our feet to the extent, as the member for Timmins pointed out, that gold mines in Timmins have had to close down.
If gold is a commodity which we can sell and is a worthwhile commodity, then let us decide nationally to support it to the extent that we can mine it or, if not, get out of the field. I suggest that, if the solution is an increase in the emergency gold mining assistance program-we are paying a large sum of money at the present time to that industry-let us do it in such a way that part of it will go to the miners in the form of wages and part of it to the communities to enable them to pay the taxes to operate the municipalities rather than make it necessary for the people living there to pay abnormally high taxes to support education in areas in

DEBATES	March 3, 1966
other parts of Canada when they are not going to get the benefit of the training that is not now being provided in all the northern areas. Had we done this in the first place, sums of money would have been available to the gold mining communities of northern Ontario to enable the industry to pay wages and subsidize the maintenance of new industries until they were vibrant.
There are other industries in the mining field which have not received much assistance. One of them is the silver industry. I can remember Mr. Lynch, the former president now deceased, of Siscoe Mines going before the United States Senate and the United States House of Representatives and telling them that if they did not face the problem of finding a method to allow silver to seek its natural level they were going to have to debase their coinage. They have now had to do this, as Canada will have to do as well, because they did not take the advice of the people who were completely familiar with the history of the silver mining industry and the maintenance of sound solid sterling currency in their own countries.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
The silver mining industry in Canada has been a very important industry. It has made Bay Street, it has made St. James Street, it has made fortunes and has supported many industries in all parts of Canada, as has the gold mining industry. I think these industries deserve some guarantee as to their future just as I believe the gold mining industry deserves some guarantee as to its future. The solution to this problem is easy and can be effected in my area if the government has the guts and courage to take action.
There is a new captive iron mine opening in my area which is owned by a Pittsburgh steel company. I suggest that the production of iron in that area has been subsidized in many ways, including cheap transportation over our provincially owned railway, to such an extent that we receive no royalty at all for the iron taken out of the ground. The only benefit we receive in this regard is employment for 200, 300 or 400 people in the area. It seems to me that if this industry was operated properly and a steel mill was established in northern Ontario there would be jobs for 2,000 to 5,000 individuals, each of whom would pay provincial taxes, municipal taxes and federal taxes. I am sure in this way the money necessary to develop that steel industry would be repaid in less than 20 years.
March 3, 1966

Do we want a Canada or are we just to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the United States? We are going to have to think about this. I agree with everyone who says that one small mine will not support a steel mill but a Timagami mine is being opened by Dofasco. I refer to the Sherman mine, It is to be financed independently and has no captive-market. It is going to sell its own ore. This ore could go to a most lucrative market if there was a steel plant in that area.
The minister from the Maritimes is interested in developing projects in the Maritimes.
I suggest he has a difficult proposition because he has not faced the problem referred to by a previous speaker, that is, where are the markets to be? We have markets in northern Ontario for steel to meet Canadian demands which are not being met in Canada today. We have iron ore right at Cochrane. There are two or three deposits in my riding and there are deposits across the border in Quebec. I suggest there are enough iron ore deposits in my part of northern Ontario to supply such a steel mill for the next 50 years, but even that amount would not satisfy the entrepreneurs who would develop this steel mill. They would need a longer guarantee of supply than 50 years.
If we want to develop a long range steel production project in Canada we should consider the iron ore deposits on Belcher Island in Hudson Bay. There is enough iron ore there to make it economically feasible to bring it to northern Ontario to supply a steel mill there for at least another 50 or possibly 100 years. When that iron ore has been used I am sure there will be much more found in that area because in my opinion the surface has only been scratched.
Such a project could be carried out if the government really wanted to do something in this way, but it will have to put up the money. I don't give a damn who runs the mill, whether it be private industry or the government. I could not care less. But there are legitimate reasons why the company that already has a mill established in Pittsburgh will pay any type of premium and make any kind of investment to obtain a captive mine in Canada, particularly when the government makes arrangements for the iron ore to be transferred to the United States at the lowest possible cost. I do not blame the entrepreneur in Pittsburgh in this regard but I believe that if we are really anxious to be Canadians and have Canadian industries we are going to have to put up some money.
DEBATES	2139
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys
I have heard a lot of wisecracks made by western members about the steel mill in Regina. I suggest that if there ever was an illogical place to put a steel mill it is on the baldheaded prairies where there is no market and no iron ore. However, a steel mill was established there with government support for the simple reason that the west needed steel to develop an industrial empire on the prairies. The provincial government put up money to make sure that a steel plant was developed there. Sdme may point out that there have been difficulties encountered since its construction but steel is being manufactured on the baldheaded prairies. In my opinion that is not a place where the officials of the Department of Industry would recommend that a steel mill be built because you cannot establish an industry unless you have the basic materials and resources in the area where it is to be established. You also require a consumer market.
I suggest that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys has been a useless asset over the years so far as the communities of northern Ontario are concerned. It is true that the department has done a great deal more in other fields than mining, and much of the difficulty has revolved around the fact that natural resources come within provincial jurisdiction. For that reason the provincial departments of mines have a much greater responsibility than the federal department. On the other hand, I do not believe the people in Toronto would try to discourage the federal government if it were willing to invest money to develop the industry in northern Ontario. I am sure they would not be in disagreement provided it did not cost them anything.
I used the iron ore industry as an example but what I have said is also true of the copper industry in the Timmins area. This is also true of zinc and silver mines. It is interesting to note that the Timmins area will provide a great amount of ore over a long period of time and will have great influence on copper production in Canada. I think it is a disgrace if the companies involved are allowed to export this raw material to other countries.
The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has been interested in the export of ore from Canada. I am sure he is aware of what happened in Australia not long ago when the government told a Japanese company that it could take part of the ore mined in Australia out of the country if
2140	COMMONS
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys in return it developed a processing mill in Australia. The government told that company that if it did not agree to these terms it could not take any ore. Why should we be so generous with the United States because the interested people there have a few bucks? Are we willing to sell our souls, our Canadian nationalism and our Canadian nationhood for a few dollars and cents? I am sure if you ask that question of the businessmen of this country their answer will be yes, as long as they pay us more bucks than we can get in Canada. I do not think that is true of the Canadian public and I hope to God it is not true of the Canadian government. Surely it is time now for some of our government officials to stand up and say that this is not true.
We hear a lot of talk about gold and silver and the fact that they are only precious metals which do not make the wheels of industry go around, but there are a lot of people engaged in space exploration who will tell you that without silver there would not be much activity in that field. I think that argument can be carried into the basic metals industry. We have an abundance of these metals in northern Ontario.
I have often said that we should not be interested in moving people from one industrial area to another. We must bring industry to the areas where these people live. You can say that the people who live on Belle Isle are poor and depressed, you can say that the people of the Maritimes are poor and depressed, but let me point out that some miners in northern Ontario are working underground for less than $2 an hour.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
I say that is a depressed wage. This situation creates a depressed area and something must be done for these people. I suggest that if you agree with this proposition you also have to agree that the solution is not in uprooting the people from the areas in which the mining industry has developed very up to date communities; the solution is in helping the mining industry rebuild their communities, particularly in those areas where the industry has changed and where the type of industry lends itself to the development of other industries.
The Prime Minister came into northern Ontario. I had the benefit of having him start his campaign in my riding. I hasten to say that I do not disagree with what the Prime Minister said in my riding, because he said he would see that something was done about industrial development in Timiskaming. He

DEBATES	March 3, 1966
said he would do something for the farmers in Timiskaming. He said he would help industry develop in northern Ontario. With these objectives I agree. I suggest that if a Liberal or a Conservative had been elected in Timiskaming they also would have come to Ottawa and demanded government assistance to develop the industries of our area.
The people of northern Ontario, no matter with what political party they are affiliated, are first northerners and second politicians. I believe they are all convinced that if we in northern Ontario are to survive something must be done for the industries in this area. Certainly the Minister of National Health and Welfare knows something of this problem because he had something to do with it. He knows there is a great reluctance on the part of the people of northern Ontario to move out of this part of the country into the cities, even though the jobs there pay a great deal more money. He knows it is difficult to move people from Glace Bay into Toronto and Montreal. He knows it is difficult to move people from any area in which they live and have been raised if they are satisfied with everything in the area but the lack of business and employment opportunities. If the minister agrees with what I have said, he has no alternative in my opinion but to support the proposition that the federal government through the Department of Labour, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Department of Industry, should take the resources that we have, subsidize them if necessary, and create around them viable industries that will grow and develop in the area. If private industry does not do it, I suggest that the governments of the provinces in co-operation with the federal government will have to do it.
I am very pleased to live right on the border of the province of Quebec because I have heard that their Minister of Resources, Mr. Rene Levesque, went into Noranda and told one of the richest, most despotic and dictatorial companies ever to exist on the North American continent that if they did not do something to improve wages in the base metal industry he would do something about it, and nationalize them. I do not think he has to nationalize them; all he has to do is threaten to do so.
It is about time this government considered what happened there, because the company settled its differences with labour very shortly afterwards. Mr. Levesque called both labour and management representatives to
March 3, 196G

Quebec city and told them, "Sit down and negotiate a solution to these differences or I will run your mines and make the decisions for you". We are told that this is a government of free enterprisers, if there is such an animal left. Free enterprisers is a term applied to the gold mines, because we give them a million bucks a month to run the business they want. Yet, they are not willing to pay proper wages to their employees or contribute anything to the well-being of the community.
I come from a community in which one individual has made millions of dollars but has not put one red cent into the community. He did build lovely parks in Welland and established beautiful estates in Bermuda, but he did not put one cent into the community in the form of assistance. Yet these are the people we are willing to subsidize, not the workers, communities or industries that are capable of developing.
The government says this area does not meet the criteria. Criteria be damned; the Department of Industry has no criteria. The Prime Minister sits down with the Premier of Ontario; they play shuffleboard with the criteria and decide, "This place in my riding will be designated and in return I will designate one area in your riding". Is that applying criteria? It is about time we threw this idea of criteria out the window and decided to do something fundamental in regard to developing industry. This can be done. It has been done in the Scandinavian countries.
I do not think I should agree to any concessions in regard to the departments which we are considering because this government has not through its ministers made any concrete proposals in keeping with the suggestions the Prime Minister made in my riding, when he promised he would help solve the problems of the distressed areas, those of the gold mining industry and the lumber industry, and establish a program for the base metal industry that would provide the people there with more than minimum wages for digging out the minerals.
The mineral wealth of northern Ontario is beyond comprehension. I do not think there is any geologist in Canada who would dare to estimate in hundreds of billions of dollars the amount of mineral wealth that will come out of northern Ontario in the next 100 years. In return for this great potential I believe we the people of northern Ontario, yes, we the people of Canada, deserve action on the part of the government to assist this
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys industry. Something should be done about developing the natural resources of our nation for the betterment of the people of Canada.
I certainly hope that the minister who is going to represent northern Ontario, whether he be from Montreal or Vancouver, will stand up and say he is prepared to recommend to the government that they do something about the desecration of our raw materials in northern Ontario and help us produce the wealth which is there and get the benefit in Canada of the wealth we are producing.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few briefs remarks at this time and ask the ministers responsible whether the federal government has taken the necessary steps to see that the waters which flow into and make up the South Saskatchewan river will have strict controls placed on them as to water pollution substances.
As everyone knows, the dam being built on the South Saskatchewan river will create a large lake practically in the centre of southern Saskatchewan. It is of great importance that these waters be kept free of all pollution, because if they are not the lake that will be created could become a natural cesspool in years ahead.
We hope the federal government has a rigid pollution policy that is acceptable to the provincial governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta so that the necessary safeguards can be applied in order to keep these waters relatively free of all pollution. Saskatchewan has waited many years for this project to become a reality and waits with pride and expectation to the time when it will have a recreational area in what was once considered a dust bowl in Saskatchewan. This lake will be used as a recreational area by many people from all parts of Canada in years to come.
For this reason I would plead with the federal government to put into effect a rigid water pollution policy governing these waters as well as other waterways in western Canada. I would expect that if the federal government takes the initiative they will receive the co-operation of the provincial governments concerned. This is of importance at this time because the lake has started to become a reality and steps should be taken now regarding water pollution.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
