speechtext:
I wish to make a few remarks on the estimates of the Department
March 3, 1966
2142	COMMONS
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys of Mines and Technical Surveys. First of all,
I should like to refer briefly to the words of the Minister of National Health and Welfare when he mentioned the hon. member for Cape Breton South. He said the member had not brought forward any constructive ideas about coal mining in the province of Nova Scotia in this or any other Parliament. I remind the minister, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, the hon. member for Cape Breton South and myself come from coal mining areas. The very fact that these members have been sent here by their constituents shows that they have a right to get up in this house and speak on behalf of their constituents. The hon. member for Cape Breton South is well versed in the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia, having worked in the mines. The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria broke his back working in a coal mine. I worked in a mine, too, and although I do not know how much coal I got out, I was brought up in a coal mining family, a fact of which I am very proud.
May I just remind the minister we are not back in the old days of the former Liberal regime, when our people came to Ottawa with their hats in their hands to see the great white father. This idea went out the window in 1957. At that time, I was pleased to come to Ottawa, with my two colleagues, and put forward representations from the coal mining areas. We intend to carry on for some time to come.
You ask, what is the problem in the coal mining industry? The hon. member for Ti-miskaming thought that perhaps markets were our problem. Until a few years ago this was the case. I am going to quote briefly from the Dominion Coal Board report for 1964-1965, page 10, where I find this:
Coal production in Nova Scotia in the year under review was 4,316,000 tons. The decrease of 159,000 tons reflected circumstances at the mines and failure to meet production targets, not lack of markets.
The report goes on to point out that the trouble with our mines is their inability to generate the capital required for a systematic renewal of equipment. In other words, there are two problems. This fact was pointed out in a brief presented by the United Mine Workers of America not long ago when they appeared before the provincial government at Halifax. I believe they want to come up and visit this government. The minister asks the question, what is the hurry? I think there
[Mr. MacEwan.l

have been a lot of resolutions coming from Cape Breton. I received a copy of one from the Sydney Board of Trade. The people of Cape Breton, the people of Nova Scotia, are getting most impatient. They want to see this undertaking commenced immediately.
There are two problems. There is the matter of the older mines in which it is costly to produce coal, and there is the matter of setting up new mines, which will provide enough coal to satisfy the markets which we have. Perhaps in this regard I could point out briefly the problem in my own constituency. In that area, we have two independent mines. I hope the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys will not forget to give assistance to the independent mines. There is one mine owned by Dosco, the McBean mine which, according to the latest figures has a life of approximately three years. I am glad to report that just last week the United Mine Workers of America executive met with the officials of the department of mines and with the United Mine Workers executive in my own area, and a decision was made to do some drilling in that area in order to find new seams to open up a new mine in the Pictou County area. I do not expect the minister, or indeed our Nova Scotia minister, to do anything at this time except co-operate with the provincial government in order to find a possible opening in that area.
I made a statement on this matter before coming to Ottawa, and I attempted to raise it in the house. However, I was ruled out of order by Mr. Speaker. I fell that the federal government should provide assistance to find an opening in our area. I am led to believe that $25 million will be necessary for the modernization of the mines in the Cape Breton area and the new opening at Lingan. I am asking for an additional amount to assist in the opening of a new seam in the Pictou County area. The McBean mine employs about 400 men. During the last few years we have secured new industry in the area, namely the Scott Paper Company pulp mill, as well as the Clairtone Sound Corporation. I know that this company intends to venture into colour television sets in the spring. As has been pointed out, and this is most important, we cannot replace present industry with other industry. We must keep our present industry as well as get new ones. I put before the minister, and indeed before our Nova Scotia minister, the necessity for a guarantee that there will be adequate assistance for a possible opening in our area.
March 3, 1966	COMMONS
The cost of our coal is high. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, we had some contracts during the last few years with the Ontario Hydro Commission. These have been a great help and we hope they will continue.
I believe, as was pointed out by the efficient chairman of the Dominion Coal Board at the meeting in Victoria, that our hope for years to come for the production of power is in the thermal plants. As pointed out in the Dominion Coal Board report, this substantial rise in bituminous consumption largely reflects the accelerating rate at which coal is now being used in Canada for electric power generation. So far as I have been able to ascertain in my research, this is the area toward which most authorities in Canada look today in the matter of coal production. Our hope lies in supplying coal for the production of power in thermal power plants. My own area has one such plant, at Trenton which I hope will be enlarged. It is for this reason I am pressing for the new opening. This plant has used a great deal of coal in the last few years and it looks as if it will use more.
We do not have a sufficient supply of coal to look after our domestic needs, so we have to import coal from the former Island of Cape Breton. Certainly, we like to use that coal. I do not know whether it generates any more coal dust than was generated in the chamber this afternoon. In any event, I want to agree with my two friends, the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria and the hon. member for Cape Breton South, whom I will call the coal dust twins. I completely endorse the remarks they made in this debate.
In conclusion, I will turn from coal for a minute to the matter of technical surveys. I am going to make a speech which I have made in this house every year since I have come here. It will only take two or three minutes. I refer to the Canadian hydrographic survey ship Acadia which has been berthed in my riding at Pictou since 1947, along with the C.H.S. Cartier, which probably will not be used too much longer and is now on the Great Lakes. I have been referring to this subject since Hon. Paul Comtois was minister and visited our area and the coal mine where my father was the manager. I have pointed out to successive governments that the berthing of this ship in that area during the winter period when it is not used, has certain advantages.

The crews are located there, they have their homes there. The local shipyards have an opportunity to do the refit work and the local suppliers provide supplies. I hope that the minister will read these remarks in Hansard and that these ships will continue to be berthed in the port of Pictou.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
Before I close, sir, perhaps I could recall to mind a song with twenty some verses concerning coal mining, one verse of which went something like this:
Down in the coal mine underneath the ground,
Little rays of sunshine never can be found.
Little dusty diamonds shining all around,
Down in the coal mine underneath the ground.
We members who came from that area- the minister himself comes from a coal mining area-know what this means. We must keep those little dusty diamonds shining all around.

Mr. Chairman, I hope you will not be too hasty in calling me to order if I preface the few remarks I want to make by quoting a section from the Fisheries Act. Section 61 says, in part:
Every person who causes or knowingly permits to pass into, or puts or knowingly permits to be put, lime, chemical substances or drugs, poisonous matter, dead or decaying fish, or remnants thereof, mill rubbish or sawdust or any other deleterious substance or thing, whether the same is of the like character to the substances named in this section or not, in any water frequented by fish, is liable, for the first offence, to a penalty of twenty five dollars and costs-
The section then goes on to provide that for second and third offences the penalties will be increased.
The reason I have quoted that section of the Fisheries Act is that as far I am aware that is the principle, and almost the only, piece of legislation in the federal sphere that deals directly with the question of the pollution of the water resources of our country. I have quoted it because there is a reaction, and a very understandable reaction, on the part of the people who find serious pollution at their doorsteps, immediately to say "There should be a law which stops this''. Up to a point I think this is certainly true. However, I would agree with opinions which I know are held by other members of the house, that this is not the only and the complete solution to this question.
I am sorry that the minister who is to become the minister of energy and resources and who will take a particular interest in this matter in the future is not with us today, but

March 3. 1966
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys I am glad the minister who is taking his place for the time being happens to be the minister who has had the matter of water resources under his jurisdiction up till the present time, and is therefore familiar, not only in his capacity as minister but also, I am sure, in his capacity-to go back to a reference which was made a little earlier-as minister from British Columbia, with the importance not only of the question of the general use of our water resources, but also the question of conservation in the sense of avoiding the ever increasing pressure to pollute those resources.
When we were considering the estimates of the Department of Industry the other night, and there was considerable discussion about designated areas, I suggested that as far as some communities in Canada were concerned they should perhaps be designated as areas rapidly becoming unfit for human habitation, because of the level to which pollution of the water and also of the air was reaching.
I have been seeking some information about the activities in which the federal government has been engaging to deal with this question, in particular its activities in the field of research. The Minister of Industry, when I raised the question in respect of the activities of the National Research Council, said that he would inform himself and then inform me. Possibly the minister who is piloting these estimates through may be a little more immediately knowledgeable on this question, and if he has some information on this subject which he could briefly give the committee I for one would certainly welcome it while the subject matter of this department is before us.
I would draw to his attention, as I did to the attention of the Minister of Industry, the fact that I have on the order paper a question which was put there on February 9-perhaps that is not an undue length of time in view of the nature of the question-and which asks for specific information about what is being done by various departments or agencies of the federal government in the field of pollution control research.
I am not going to attempt at this time to launch into this question with the eloquence with which the hon. member for Timis-kaming made his plea for development of the mining industry in northern Ontario. If the minister from the maritimes whom he named would ship some of his coal to the smelter in northern Ontario, then if they run out of iron ore perhaps I could send some iron ore from

my constituency to the maritimes, this would provide a real example of national development and unity, and incidentally provide a lot of business for the railways. However that may not be the most feasible solution to that particular problem.
One other question I would specifically like the minister to answer relates to a forthcoming event of which I know he is fully aware. I refer to the conference to be held this fall in Montreal on the subject of pollution and our environment, under the sponsorship of the Canadian Council of Resource Ministers.
I have in my hand a pamphlet which indicates some of the details of the planning of this conference. It also indicates that a brochure is being prepared and distributed, outlining further details. This brochure is being distributed throughout Canada to interested governments, institutions, associations and individuals. Then it goes on to say that invitations to the conference will be extended by the federal and provincial governments.
One of the questions I should like to have answered is whether or not the government of Canada is going to extend such invitation to members of parliament who might be interested in participating in that conference. I find myself rather impatient, even though I recognize there are some complexities in planning this matter, at the fact that we are not any further along the way toward an effective dealing with the acute problems of pollution which exist in some areas, including at least two areas in my constituency which I could name, than to be thinking about a discussion or a study conference on the subject next fall.
Nevertheless, from what little reading I have done about the planning for this conference, I readily agree that there may be some quite worth-while things come out of it. I only hope that its results will reflect themselves very quickly in effective action both at the federal and at the provincial levels of government.
The bulletin to which I referred earlier contains this statement, made by the man who I believe is currently chairman of the Resource Ministers Council. He says:
The continuing pollution of our water, of our air and of our soil rests upon our conscience. It is a problem to which every Canadian must turn his attention.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, this is a statement with which a great many of my constituents would agree. I do want to say, without further
March 3, 1966

prolonging my comments, that a good many of my constituents are becoming increasingly impatient with the continuance of the situation, and the conditions under which they have to live. Unless some effective action is forthcoming rather speedily following this conference, they are going to become even more impatient than they are at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize that the committee wants to get on with the passing of these estimates, and I as a member of the official opposition on this side of the house have refrained from taking part in the debate so far. However, I should be remiss in my duty to my constituents if I did not direct a few remarks to the minister about the development of heavy water in Canada. Recently, when I directed this question to the Minister of Industry I was informed that it did not come under his purview. I feel justified in bringing the matter before the committee at this particular time.
Just to recall a few of the facts, hon. members may remember that this matter was introduced by the Minister of Industry one year ago last November, at which time he went through the process of explanation in the house. It was stated, and carried forward then, that a heavy water plant in Canada was nearing completion at Glace Bay, Nova Scotia. The minister announced that a market was available; that it was time Canada took steps to see that a second heavy water plant was developed. Tenders were called and, I believe on January 29, 1965, which was the deadline, four responsible companies made a bid. I think all members of the house will recall the excitement and anticipation engendered in certain areas that thought they might be affected by this development. There was much excitement and approval at Estevan as a result of that announcement. Estevan is in the province of Saskatchewan, and I make these remarks because of the importance of this subject to my riding.
Hon. members may recall that Estevan was selected as the site for the erection of this heavy water plant, as a result of a supplementary statement by the minister. Naturally as a result of the minister's statement that Estevan, Saskatchewan, was the site and Western Deuterium Limited of British Columbia, the successful bidder, the city immediately took steps to be prepared for this development.

Considerable sums of money were spent; facilities were built to accommodate the extra industrial and technical populace which would be coming in to develop this plant, which it was anticipated would take three years to complete, and which would have from 500 to 1,000 workmen working on it. The city aldermen and various other authorities took steps to improve facilities such as sewers, water, and the like.
Then it was realized, in July 1965 to the great consternation of the city of Estevan, that Western Deuterium Limited was not going on with the proposed plant. The authorities in the city were under the impression that a positive announcement had been made by the minister about the development, similar to that made with respect to the heavy water plant at Glace Bay.
It turned out that although Western Deuterium Limited had acted properly, there was nothing cut and dried. The whole scheme was just a proposal, and must have been a premature announcement on the part of the government. It was to be, in the first place, an announcement of policy. If that announcement had been cut and dried, and the contract to develop heavy water undertaken, things would have turned out differently. Naturally we are still very much interested in this. After that, when inquiries were made, we learned that Atomic Power Corporation of Calgary, the second lowest bidder, would be invited to take over the contract of Western Deuterium Limited. This also failed to carry through.
Then, the latest information was that Canadian General Electric of Peterborough were invited, some three months ago, to make a follow-up survey of the prospects of building a second heavy water plant, and of discussing as soon as possible where it should be constructed.
I have done my best to inquire into the determinations of this policy. A lot of money has been spent in my constituency, and there is still a vague shadow over the policy surrounding this proposed project.
I would ask the minister if he could advise this committee now as to what actually is the status of this heavy water plant, and when it is expected to have something finalized about it. I am sure that the people of Saskatchewan and the people of Estevan Point, Saskatchewan, are very much interested, as I think the government is. I hope we shall hear something definite before long, because the people

I should like to make a few brief comments relating to the remarks of hon. members opposite this afternoon and evening. First of all I should like to say that we listened with great interest to the contribution made by the hon. member for Kamloops. We do not disagree with much of what he said. We believe that Canada's future depends on what type of national resources policy we have in Canada, and that Canadian identity is closely linked to that resources policy. I am sure the hon. member knows that the minister of northern

affairs and I are on record in respect of this subject.
We believe in a national resources policy. We believe in a co-ordinated policy between federal and provincial governments for the development and management of our water, our soil, our air and our minerals. We believe that this national policy must be achieved in co-operation with the provinces, but by way of a national catalyst or initiative-by federal co-ordination with the provinces on policies achieved on a national basis.
We believe also, Mr. Chairman, that the growth of Canada depends on development on a national basis of our natural and renewable resources. Although I will deal with this more specifically, I want to say to the hon. member for Timiskaming that in our vocabulary, this growth must be developed profitably for all Canadians in Canada. This is true of everything that we have on and under the ground and in the water. We believe that the development of a national resources policy includes as a corollary a resources policy for all of Canada and particularly for the northern areas of the country.

I admit that and I shall discuss later the particular problem of the member for Villeneuve.

I suggest that we need national co-ordination of various provincial policies. We need research into what we are doing because facts must precede policy. We believe that an inventory, as mentioned by the hon. member for Kamloops and others, is absolutely a prerequisite to such a policy. We need at the same time to develop a cost benefit ratio for the development of these resources and to set priorities, if necessary, on a national scale as to the resources we can profitably bring into production in series.
I should like to list the steps of what we conceive to be a national resources policy for this country. First of all we have to make an inventory of these resources. There are already programs in this country for the setting up or establishment of a Canadian land inventory. I feel we also have to proceed with an evaluation of our water resources and needs. We must analyse the quality of the air above us, and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni made special reference to that. So we are talking in terms of an inventory of our
March 3, 1966	COMMONS DEBATES	2151
forests, lands, recreation fisheries and wildlife and, particularly within the text of this department, our mineral resources.
After having made that inventory we conceive that Canada must have co-ordinated management of those resources, and that the federal government must achieve through the national council of resource ministers some standardization of inventory and management, as well as some recognition of the amount of budgetary support that each province will have to devote to the development of any particular resource.
Once the inventory and co-ordinated management policy have been worked out with the provinces, we believe that priorities related to production ought to be established between those resources and various areas so that the development of these resources can follow. We believe this should be linked with a policy directed toward increasing the processing of these resources in Canada. We believe also that a deliberate national development of resources depends on certain ancillary policies, and that we must co-ordinate our tariff policies so the whole range and purpose becomes consistent with what we are trying to achieve.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Taxation must reflect this policy as well, and tax abatement and accelerated tax depreciation must be co-ordinated with the development of those resources. Fiscal and monetary policy can also be used to the same effect, as can transportation policy, whereby the government of Canada provides access to markets and access to development by road, rail, water and air. In this connection, Mr. Chairman, I want to recognize the tremendous results of the Roads to Resources policy initiated by the previous administration. In other words, resource development in our vocabulary means growth, and growth means manufacturing complexes within Canada, bringing employment and people with them.
Turning to another point raised by the hon. member for Kamloops, with which we disagree, he pointed out that to his mind the setting aside of the resource development north of the 60th parallel and leaving it with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources lacked consistency, because if Canada were to have a co-ordinated national resource policy the resources of the north should be brought under the jurisdiction of the new minister of energy, mines and resources. I suppose we might discuss with
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys profit on some other occasion the difference between the policy of the management of those resources and their administration. speechtext:
With the spirit of co-operation that prevails in this chamber tonight, I think we can safely conclude we will be able to complete the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs by the time we are ready to rise at the normal hour at ten o'clock. I think I should point out that the members of the opposition, in co-operating in this fashion, do not want in any respect to neglect a thoroughgoing discussion of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, as it used to be. We are co-operating because of our desire to help out the government which, as a result of its own maladministration, has boxed itself into this unfortunate position. We are also co-operating because we are so far behind in the schedule for the consideration of the 1965-66 estimates. We realize, however, that it will be only a comparatively short time before we will have an opportunity for a thoroughgoing discussion on the reorganized Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
This department has had a rather checkered career since it was first inaugurated in 1952. When I was the minister responsible for
March 3, 1966

it there were many interesting facets of operation and administration that were not directly concerned with northern affairs or even resources, as such. It had come out of the old department of resources and now, if all goes well in the reorganization contemplated, a good part of the administrative responsibilities of northern affairs will return to the new department of resources. I believe without prejudice we can say that many of the functions that came out of the old department of resources are returning to the new department of resources in a considerably enhanced state. I was pleased to hear the Minister without Portfolio in his brief enunciation of the schemes and programs contemplated to achieve a co-ordinated national resource policy indicate that they stemmed Erom the blueprint that was laid down by the former administration.
My colleague the hon. member for Kamloops has dealt with, and I feel adequately, :he problems of resource developments as :hey refer to power and water resources. These policies again were laid down with considerable care and detail by the former administration. There has been a slowing iown of the forward momentum during the past two years and I hope that with the [DOT]eorganization contemplated the pace will ;tep up once again.
I would just like to repeat for the sake of brevity tonight the three fundamental points hat emerged out of the Resources for To-norrow conference in 1961 and which were aid down by the then Prime Minister, the 'ight hon. member for Prince Albert, when ae recommended the establishment of a na-ional resource council, the establishment of a lational advisory land and water use co-irdinating board and the convening of peri-idic conferences in the field of resource man-igement. We have the Resource Ministers Council functioning as an organization. Un-ortunately there have been difficulties be-ause of frequent personnel changes among he staff of the secretariat. I do hope, in the nterests of continuity and in the interests of o-ordination, that we will be able to gather ogether a permanent secretariat of the high-st possible qualifications who can get on /ith the job of assisting in the task of wise lanagement and the multiple use of Cana-a's resources.
However, nothing has been done with re-pect to the National Advisory Council of fater Resources. This was regarded as a
Supply-Northern Affairs fundamental necessity in 1961. The need has become more urgent in the intervening five years and the problem now, is recognized by all concerned as having long passed the point of no return. I remember some two years ago when this party moved an amendment to the motion to go into supply which recommended the establishment of an advisory co-ordinating committee of water resources, that several members from various parts of the house, as well as the press, yawned in boredom because they believed that the subject of conversation of water resources as a topic for a supply amendment was moving into an area in which there was a complete lack of necessity for discussion. This was only two years ago; but since that time we have had views from many groups in the country urging immediate action to get a national perspective on the management of our water resources.
I trust that under the new reorganization contemplated, Mr. Chairman, this point No. 2, which I think was just as important as and which indeed springs out of the establishment of the National Resource Ministers Council, will be given primary consideration. Indeed it is unfortunate that the National Resource Ministers Council itself has not come to grips with the establishment of such a national advisory committee on the management of our water resources. That is all I intend to say on this subject at this time.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
The third point is of course being carried out in the pollution conference which will be held in Montreal under quite similar circumstances to the original conference in 1961. This is the first convening of a conference dealing with specific areas of renewable resources since 1961. It is a five-year interval and I hope in the future we will be able to move at a much more rapid pace.
Now coming specifically to northern affairs,
I am going to cut down my remarks and deal with only two aspects of current responsibility. As in the past, when we had responsibility for administration, we carried out policies on an organized and co-ordinated basis. I am therefore going to call upon my colleague from the Yukon Territory who win deal with some of the specifics of northern administration. I am sure we all agree there is no one in the house more competent or qualified to speak on this subject, and certainly no one in this chamber who has made a greater contribution to bringing the needs and problems of the north
2154	COMMONS
Supply-Northern Affairs to the attention of this house as well as to the attention of the people of Canada as a whole.
I shall depend on my hon. friend from Jasper-Edson to deal with the current problems through which parks are passing.
There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister of northern affairs which I feel indicates shortsightedness and that lack of the vision which is necessary if the program of northern development that was launched with such great enthusiasm in 1957 is to contine to move forward.
I refer to the decision to change the location of the new administrative headquarters for the department of northern affairs. At the time we left office the decision had been made to add the new northern affairs building to the interesting complex that had been developing in that section of the city of Ottawa known as Confederation Heights. It seemed entirely fitting to me as the minister responsible that the department which had to do with the development of Canada's last frontier should occupy an important and prominent position among the complex of buildings at Confederation Heights. As the current minister knows, plans were finalized and completed to proceed with the construction of a building that would not only be useful and functional but also symbolic of the fact that Canada is a northern nation with a northern heritage and a northern destiny.
We wondered why the delay in proceeding with this particular project. The story has now become available in the current report of the Auditor General, which indicates that the minister made the decision to continue the location of the northern affairs headquarters in the heart of the nation's capital on the ground that our administrative facilities were becoming too widely scattered; that everything should be crowded into the downtown area. This seems to me to be entirely the antithesis of the thinking of a department which concerns itself with the development of the last frontier, the wide open spaces, the million and a half square miles of area which makes up the Northwest Territories and the Yukon territory.
I have been continually amazed since I came to Ottawa as a member of parliament in the early fifties to understand why those who are responsible for the planning of the nation's capital have such a myopic and narrow perspective of architectural development and city planning prospects. It seems that unless
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
DEBATES	March 3, 1966
everything is crowded within a few blocks of Parliament Hill, then we have not got the proper planning perspective.
In visiting other capitals, for example the capital of our neighbour to the south, the attractive feature of the city of Washington in the District of Columbia is the wide open thoroughfares and spaces which have been made possible by deliberate planning in consonance with the broad developmental viewpoint of the United States administration.
It is a retrograde and a backward step to reverse the decision to locate northern affairs in what was regarded as the most strategic location site of Confederation Heights. Overlooking the R.A. Centre and facing towards the north, what could be more symbolic of the new forward step in the nation's thinking and planning? The change was made at considerable expense to the public treasury, as the Auditor General pointed out. The architects' fees had already been paid and the plan had to be scrapped. As I recall, some $200,000 went down the drain.
The new building is not owned, it is rented. It is the Campeau Confederation Towers. It borrows the name from Confederation Heights but has the confederation symbolism in name only because it certainly does not carry the architectural and planning motif that is present in the Confederation Heights development. I understand the buildings are rented, according to the Auditor General's report, at an annual rental of $688,000, almost double the rental formerly paid for northern affairs facilities in Ottawa.
Even though the responsibilities of northern affairs have diminished substantially, with museums departing, with resources departing, with water resources departing, with tourism departing, as well as other areas of responsibility, the cost of rental has doubled.

I know that the decision has been made and that the move has been made. But I suggest to the minister that he might well review and consider the original plan for the new building, and when the five-year period has expired-I believe the lease is for five years, renewable for ten-he might then reconsider the prospects of reverting to what I felt was an excellent plan in harmony with the functions of the department of northern affairs. There are one or two further brief matters. As I have already intimated, my hon. friend from Jasper-Edson will be dealing in some detail with parks. However, I repeat once again what should be entirely obvious to everybody concerned in these matters, namely that there is a great and urgent need for expanding Canada's park facilities. The pressure on our national parks is reaching beyond the point of endurance, month after month, year after year, yet no dynamic steps are being taken to deal with the urgent demands of an age of leisure as well as the growing economic demands of a rapidly expanding tourist industry.
As I have told the minister and his colleagues in the government times beyond number, it is high time we got cracking, to use a good air force phrase, on a recreational parks development program, something which was in the works when the government changed but on which no specific action has been taken.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I notice the National and Provincial Parks Association in the current edition of their excellent magazine, put forward a program of their own, which they call the Recreational Parks Development Program. They say it is an entirely new idea. With respect, it is not a new idea. They talk about it as a national recreational reserves development program. Now that we have the support of that group primarily concerned with the development of our park resources, I trust that we will at long last have the ear of the administration.
I want to ask questions now about historic parks. A program was launched, in 1961, to ensure that there would be a major historic park development in each of the provinces and the territories to make sure that parks would be available for the influx of visitors during our centennial year.
Supply-Northern Affairs
We are hearing how much Expo '67 will cost. How much is it now? It goes up day by day. An hon. member tells me that the cost will be $84 million. What will visitors coming to Canada to take part in the celebration of 1967 do, after they have seen the great centennial world fair? They are going to spread out across the rest of Canada, we hope. I should like to remind the administration that we have got to present other aspects of Canadian history than will be presented at Expo '67 at such tremendous cost.
The program of developing historic sites extended, from Signal Hill in Newfoundland, Louisburg in Nova Scotia, right up to the old gold rush city, in Dawson City. Dawson City was declared an historic complex. No doubt there will be a tremendous influx of visitors into Dawson City next year.
Through the writings of Robert Service, and the writings of other famous authors such as Jack London, perhaps one of the best known sites in Canada is old Dawson City. I trust that the minister, who I understand is still responsible for these matters, will be moving forward to ensure that in each province we have a major development ready to receive the visitors. I hesitate in mentioning the keystone province, Manitoba, because I might be regarded as prejudiced in this regard.
However, I hope that Fort Garry is proceeding on target. Something that would make historic sites interesting, I think, is animation. We had planned that these historic sites would be animated much along the same lines as Fort Henry which has become one of the great tourist attractions in the province of Ontario, a tourist attraction which has been developed by the government of Ontario. 1 trust that the same sort of animation will be implemented in each of the major centres in each of the provinces.
I do not think I need take more time of the committee at this stage. I will pass the torch to my colleagues, as I have intimated. However, I did notice the minister in recent weeks and months has been making regular announcements about roads, airports, railways and so forth. I want to congratulate him on carrying the torch that was ignited by the former administration. As I look at the roads policy, announced I think during the last election compaign, and as it is presented in the current issue of the magazine North, it seems to me that I have travelled those roads before. It seems to me a regurgitation of the northern development roads policy laid down
March 3, 1366

Supply-Northern Affairs by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, and reinforced by myself when I became minister. I see no new roads indicated in the development program, as it is outlined in the magazine North. The airport construction program especially has a familiar ring.
We are flattered by your acceptance of our programs and policies. We wish you would only get on with them with the same expedition and enthusiasm that was applied during those wonderful years of 1957 to 1963.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want this evening to talk about national parks. I wish to take some time to point out that 58 per cent of the land area of the national parks of Canada is in the province of Alberta. I want to take some time because, as I mentioned in the Throne Speech debate, some 7,000 people living in the national parks in Alberta are second class citizens and do not have the rights enjoyed by the people in other parts of Canada.
For the past seven or eight months there has been a continuing fight between the minister and the people residing in the parks. On January 18, shortly after this session opened, I asked him whether he was ready to set up a committee of inquiry to study this problem, and he answered at that time as reported at page 26 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, we have had a continuing series of discussions with the people living in our national parks and have arrived at certain understandings. I cannot accept for one minute the statement made by the hon. gentleman in his question that there is great consternation in those areas.
He goes on to say:
I am stating the facts, and I am in touch with the people living in those parks.
This prompted the people in Jasper Park to send a telegram to the minister, which reads as follows:
The following is a copy wire sent to Honourable Arthur Laing this date. "Your statement appearing in January 19th Hansard regarding situation with respect to residents of Banff and Jasper Park is generally misleading because first, great consternation and uncertainty still exists among the people residing in these parks and second we are definitely out of touch with you since our last meeting took place in Jasper on September 12th 1965 without any understanding being reached".
That is the end of the telegram. There is not any understanding. There is great consternation. Both the minister and the Prime Minister in the recent election campaign assured these people that they would be given a fair hearing. I want to suggest to the minister at the outset that in view of the fact he is going to bring in national parks legislation,

he give immediate consideration to setting up a joint committee of this house and the other place to study the question of a national parks policy. I am not alone in my concern, because hon. members from Bow River, Lethbridge and Macleod are also concerned about this. It is not just our concern, it is the concern of the province of Alberta. We had something to do with getting people living in the parks to approach the premier of Alberta, to request his support in this regard.
1 am sure that the minister has recently received a copy of a brief from the minister of industry of the Alberta government. I want to quote extensively from this brief because, Mr. Chairman, it is excellent. It is a brief that I hope the minister will read carefully and will take into consideration. It reads as follows:
The thesis of this report is that National Parks Policy is unfair to the citizens of Alberta and of serious detriment to the third largest industry in the province-tourism. This conclusion applies to both the written policy and the administration of the policy by the federal department in charge.
I shall have something more to say about the administration. The brief goes on to say:
The people of Alberta are equally concerned about the contravention of citizens' rights implicit in the new policy as it affects leaseholders in the National Parks in Alberta. The legal and moral aspects of this problem have already been the subject of an urgent letter from Premier Manning to the Prime Minister, and they are dealt with in greater detail in an accompanying brief.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I want to say something with regard to the letter from the Premier of Alberta to the Prime Minister, and the Prime Minister's reply. The Prime Minister's reply showed that the right hon. gentleman is not aware of the situation. This is a continuing operation of the senior civil servants in the minister's department-a fog thrown over the facts to try to hide behind the great conservation wave, away from the basic issue. The basic issue is the question of the townsites in these parks, the question of these people who have been invited into the parks in earlier days being allowed to live in them like Canadians, with a full concept of what is meant by the national parks as their guide. We think the minister has not allowed them a fair hearing. I believe he has been taken in by the senior civil servants in his department, who have for a number of years tried to turn themselves into the commission. They do not believe there should be townsites in the national parks. They are so unaware of the
March 3, 1966

situation in Alberta that they do not appreciate the distances involved.
They have no idea about service centres in an area such as Jasper, which is 230 miles from Edmonton. They have no idea how to look after the increasing numbers of people who have come to these parts since the development of better roads. Their thinking with regard to the proper development of these parks is at cross purposes. When this party formed the government we brought out a policy of zoning, providing for wilderness, recreation and service areas. We must have zoning of this type in Jasper, Banff and Waterton.
The conservationists tell us: The wilderness will be spoiled. They say we are going to turn the parks into a Coney Island. Nonsense. Immediately we criticize the administration of the national parks we are called Coney Islanders. They have gone so far as to solicit support from the press by giving them biased material on which to write articles. They have done this, apparently, with the approval of the minister. I prefer to believe, as a westerner, that he has been taken in.
There is a better way to run our mountain national parks. And, let me say, there is no similarity whatsoever between the running of national parks such as we have in Alberta, particularly the Rocky Mountain parks, and national parks in the rest of Canada. There is no similarity at all. The National Parks Act says these areas should be set aside for the benefit and enjoyment of Canadians. What does "enjoyment" mean according to these people in the department? It means the enjoyment of nature. We need a public inquiry with regard to the interpretation of this word because the present interpretation is not the right one. I want to quote something in this regard, later, from the brief of the Alberta government. To suggest that the enjoyment of our national parks is only to enjoy nature, is nonsense according to the normal and com-monsense interpretation of the word and, I am sure, according to the interpretation which was in the minds of those who established this legislation back in 1930. Their interpretation would mean, I suggest, that we could have recreational facilities within these parks.
In our mountain national parks we have more than half the entire area of Switzerland. In Switzerland they have all these mountain resorts, five or six major towns and between five million and six million people. We have 7,000 people living in the cities in
Supply-Northern Affairs the centres of these parks, taking up one per cent of the available area. We have roads leading to only about 5 per cent of the area of these parks. Are we going to desecrate the wilderness if a program of the type advocated by some of us on this side of the house is adopted? The Parks and Recreation Association of Canada, which has supported the attitude taken by the department on occasions, has now come round to our way of thinking and suggested that part of these parks be turned into recreational reserves within the parks system. What is this if it is not zoning for recreational purposes? How far is this away from zoning for service centres?
Reference has been made to congestion in the parks. I can give the minister the whole picture. The idea that in a 4,000 square mile park where you have at the most 100 acres taken out for a townsite there is any real likelihood of spoiling the wilderness, or that you cannot have proper regulations for the development of these towns, is an absurd one. I know the parks department officials would like to see these towns moved out altogether. They fail to appreciate that Banff and Jasper were there before the parks were set up. Jasper was a railroad town, and it still is. Jasper is as concerned about keeping the concept of the national parks as are the people in the department. But the people who live in Jasper are democratic Canadians and they feel they can do a better job than the civil service can.
It comes down to the question of the townsites and how they are to be administered. The feeling became so bad in Banff that the advisory council, which is an elected body, would not talk to the minister. I could read into the record verbatim reports of that meeting; it is not of any credit to the minister. These people deserve representative government and the right to the self-determination of their local problems within their town-sites without having to come to Ottawa about every minor decision. This is only just.
What about leaseholding? The minister suddenly wants to change the system of leaseholding and prevent families concerned from building up estates within the national parks. He is going to turn our buildings into sheds or temporary structures which will last just the length of the lease, and then revert to the government. He knows that many of the services which have been provided have been supplied by family concerns, and he intends to get these people out. The parks department seems to think that everybody in
March 3, 1966

Supply-Northern Affairs Canada wants to live in the mountain parks. They will not even allow anyone who has moved out of a park for six months to be buried there. This kind of thinking is archaic. It cannot be understood by reasonable people and it is contrary to common sense.
I suggest the minister should give consideration to these points. I want to call attention to what Hon. A. R. Patrick had to say last Friday in the Alberta legislature with regard to the policies of this government:
Calling the policies "unfair to the citizens and of serious detriment to Alberta's tourist industry," they can only result in "poor construction, drab facilities and higher prices for visitors," he said.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The minister steadfastly has refused even to listen to the delegations which have come to him from Banff, Jasper and Waterton. He has convinced the Prime Minister to send this letter to the Premier saying in part-and I quote from the Prime Minister's letter to the Premier:
From this point of view I would certainly be disturbed if even the legal exercise of governmental powers resulted in the serious disturbance of any present leaseholder of park lands in his occupation of these lands or caused significant damage to the operator of any legitimate business enterprise in the parks.
What about these people who will lose their businesses, because the government has taken them over? Has this not already caused some disturbance in our national parks, and yet the Prime Minister writes that letter to our Premier. He goes on to say:
In the case of residential leaseholders they are assured of continuity of tenure for at least another 42 years with compensation at fair market value-*
This was obtained only after representation was made to the minister. Additionally in this letter he says:
In short, there seems to be no evidence that the substitution of a term of at least 42 years from the present time in lieu of the so-called perpetual renewal clauses has had any significant effect on the present day worth of the leasehold interests concerned.
Now, if anybody is going to be asked to swallow that, it is absolute nonsense, because all property in the national park has depreciated at least 20 per cent since the minister announced his policy. He knows that as also do the people in his department. The Prime Minister went on:
I do not believe there is anything in this government's policy which will prevent a continuation of the rapid growth in public use of these areas experienced in recent years.

That is absolutely false. The situation in Banff, Jasper and Waterton is at the stage where there is not sufficient accommodation for the people who go there in the summer time to service our tourists. No new lots have been made available in Banff in years. We finally have had some made available at Jasper, but there is a crying need for more accommodation in the town of Jasper; there is a crying need for land for churches and service club buildings, which it has been very difficult to get out of the department. I could go on and give examples of applications which took years to be processed through that archaic department which the minister has the honour to head.
The Prime Minister went on to say:
I can assure you that policy of this government is to depend to the greatest extent possible on the private sector of the economy to establish and operate the commercial aspects of park operations.
How are you going to get private enterprise to go in there? The park and departmental officials do not want private enterprise to go in. The senior officials of the department would like to own everything in there, and have so admitted. They would like to get rid of the school of fine arts and other activities.
The Prime Minister says to the Premier that there is no difficulty. I have a letter here from Waterton that tells us of part of the difficulty. There is no disturbance in the ordinary business in these national parks? The businessmen there are having trouble getting insurance. In a telephone call the insurance agent who handles quite a large percentage of the insurance in Waterton informed me that the owners of property in the Waterton Lake and national park area were no longer considered to be a good risk by the insurance company and that these companies would no longer give complete coverage on park property. And this did not disturb business in these parts? Surely the Prime Minister was led down the garden path in that regard.
I would hope that the minister would follow through on the pleas made in the past in respect of the national parks and that he would allow these people an inquiry here in Ottawa. I would hope that he would back up the Prime Minister in his speech in October in Calgary when he promised the people in the national parks in Alberta that they would receive a fair hearing. I suggest to the minister that with the acquisition of the three hon. gentlemen who joined the other place the other day, from the province of Alberta, that they have sufficient numbers in the other

place so that we could provide our part of the committee, and that we should form a committee to delve into this problem of national parks policy.
I believe this is necessary if we are going to develop these townsites, which will remain despite the fact that the director of the national parks does not believe that they should be there. They will remain. Let us have a realistic look at this and not just play politics with it as has been done on occasion. It is necessary to have this inquiry so that interested groups on both sides of the fence, the purists, the sensible people, the residents of the parks, the province of Alberta and other provinces which have national parks-if they are contemplating the creation of other national parks-will have an opportunity to enter into the discussions.
I suggest that now is the time to define the policy and make sure that the residents in these parks know about it, and know that it is not something that is slipped through. Let us have this committee of inquiry; let us have a joint committee of the house and the Senate set up to investigate this matter and bring in a recommendation in respect of national parks. Surely it is only right that there should be a body where interested people and groups, such as the Association of National Provincial Parks of Canada and others could come to express their views.
This is a most important matter so far as we in Alberta are concerned. The 1972 Olympics may be prejudiced by this federal policy. I am sure the officials of the department do not want to see the Olympics at Banff, but there are many of us who do and I am sure it is the general consensus on the part of the people in Canada. These are important questions in respect of the national parks, and these questions have to be resolved. It is not enough that the minister should go and fight with the advisory council in Banff, and the advisory council at Jasper and Waterton; it is not enough that he should try to push it down their throats. It is necessary that we have an inquiry and that the people have an opportunity to express their opinions before a committee. The minister did not get a standing ovation from the residents of either of the three national parks, and did not get very many votes either.

Mr. Chairman, now that we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources I should like to refer in particular to a question or two regarding Indian affairs, as the responsibility for this department was transferred to Hon. Arthur Laing earlier this year.
Before commenting on this problem in relation to the Christian Island band I should like to pay public tribute to Hon. Rene Tremblay who, for a while, was minister of immigration and Indian affairs. When the estimates of this department were being considered a year or two ago I asked the minister if he would give consideration to the very earnest request of the Ojibway Indians on the Christian Island reserve in the lower Georgian Bay area for the establishment of a radio telephone service. I pointed out at that time that the Indians were still being forced by the department of Indian affairs to communicate with the mainland by smoke signal in the same manner Indians communicated with Christopher Columbus. Hon. Mr. Tremblay immediately busied himself with that request to establish a radio telephone system connected with Midland. As a result there was established a radio-telephone service, a stop and go system, but the Indians thought it was a tremendous operation compared with the system they had been forced to use for the past 300 years. Only last fall under the able administration of the cabinet this stop and go telephone system was greatly improved and, with the co-operation of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, a mobile exchange was put on Christian Island. There are today 45 telephones in the homes of Indian families on Christian Island and they are able to communicate with people at any telephone number on the mainland, despite the separation of a mile and a half by water.
I should like to thank Hon. Rene Tremblay myself and on behalf of the Ojibway band of

the Christian Island reserve for what he did, and the cabinet for carrying on even after Rene Tremblay left the department of immigration. I feel certain that Hon. Arthur Laing will pay as much attention to their present, sensible demands as did the minister before him.
The Christian Island band of Indians, who are of the Ojibway tribe, some years ago with the very earnest co-operation of Colonel Jones, who was a senior official of the department of Indian affairs, were able to establish a pheasant farm on Christian Island. They raise about 4,000 pheasants a year and it is possible to go and hunt there for seven months of the year. You are certain that there are birds before your gun; it is not a case of going into the wilderness hoping there is game. When you go to the Christian Island reservation pheasant farm you know there are birds there which were released the day before you arrived.
The problem that is facing the Indians today is this. There is no overnight accommodation available on the island for hunting. The nearest hotel accommodation to the Christian Island reservation is at Penetan-guishene, 11 miles away. Very few hunters who go to Christian Island in the morning and have to go back to Penetang in the evening return to the island a second day. The Indians would like to have the hunters stay for two or three days at a time and they have made efforts to establish a hunters' lodge on the island, for which they could charge accommodation.
I have a letter in my hand written two weeks ago today by Chief Monague of the Beausoleil band of the Ojibway Indians on Christian Island. This letter reads:
Dear Mr. Cowan;
We had funds made available from supplement construction program and approval to erect a hunters' lodge to accommodate pheasant hunters. Some are reluctant to come, even though reservations for hunts had been made, due to the short length of time they would have here, there being no accommodations for them to stay over so that they can have a complete day. Inadequate transportation is also a source of trouble.
Since the approval and funds were made available for the lodge we have been advised that the plan has since been rejected.
I feel as if I am stepping over the heads of the Indians Affairs Branch to reconsider their decision but the Council felt that when we introduced the plans at our Council meeting this would help boost our revenue tremendously from the pheasant and tourist projects.
Please, may we have your assistance through your office to approach the Minister, Hon.
March 3, 1966

Mr. Arthur Laing, to have the Branch reconsider their ruling to our favour.
The phones are a godsend to us. the best way to contact our families who are off the Reserve. Thanking you.
Yours truly,
Leonard J. Monague Chief, Beausoleil Band.
I should like to point out that this pheasant farm, which was established originally with the co-operation of Colonel Jones under the previous administration, and which has been encouraged ever since, has been a great source of revenue to the Indians, so much so that they are now considering establishing a wild turkey farm on Hope Island, and are considering putting deer on Beckwith Island. This will give them commercial hunting revenue similar to the revenue received from some of those big game farms in the United States. When this is accomplished we will have wild turkeys available for the purpose of hunting on Hope Island and deer on Beckwith Island. I am certain that these ideas are good and that they will work.
While I am on my feet, and I only want to speak for another minute or two, I should like to suggest to the minister of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources that he give very serious consideration to the acquiring of title to Giant's Tomb Island in the lower Georgian Bay area for the purpose of a national park.
Giant's Tomb Island is the biggest island south of Manitoulin Island and it is at the present time in the hands of an estate. We now have the Beausoleil Island national park, just off from Midland. Giant's Tomb Island lies between this national park and these three Indian reservation islands, Christian Island, Beckwith Island and Hope Island.
The province of Ontario has taken a great forward step under Premier John Robarts and Kelso Roberts, the minister of lands and forests, in acquiring 2,300 acres of land on the south shore of Georgian Bay. There are plans for a provincial park on this shore property, which is opposite Giant's Tomb Island, to be known as Methodist Point provincial park.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
With Beausoleil Island already a national park, with the tremendous new provincial park which is coming up and the three Indian reservation islands, the acquisition of Giant's Tomb Island as a national park would be a mighty step forward on the part of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. The five islands I have named and the new provincial park, Methodist Point
23033-137J
Supply-Northern Affairs Park, will be within 90 miles of metropolitan Toronto with a population of two million. There will not be another large national park within the Dominion of Canada so quickly and easily available to so many people as a national park developed in the lower end of Georgian Bay.
While Giant's Tomb Island is in the hands of the estate of a lady who recently passed away I would urge very, very sincerely that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources look into the possible acquisition of this property to round out a beautiful system of national and provincial parks on the north side of Simcoe County in lower Georgian Bay. I hope the minister will make certain that the Indians are able to erect their hunters' lodge at this time. The pheasant season is open until March 31 on commercial game farms and then is closed to September 1. I trust the minister will look into my suggestion, of acquiring Giant's Tomb Island for development as a national park, in the same way as we have been operating Beausoleil Island for	the past many
years.

I believe also, though I cannot see them from where I am standing, that the three-member advisory committee on finance, all members of the Yukon Legislative Council, are here as well to discuss with
2162	COMMONS
Supply-Northern Affairs departmental officials the estimates of the Territorial government.
My remarks this evening will be directed to a matter that is becoming an increasing problem to the federal government, to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and one that is becoming one of increasing concern to the people of the Yukon and Northwest Territories. I was going to make some remarks in connection with the hon. member for Northwest Territories, but I shall refrain from doing that until another time when he is in the chamber to hear them.
I believe the minister will agree with me that one of the most important features of any democratic institution is the amalgamation of the executive with the legislative arm of government. The progress which has been made toward that end in the Yukon Territory, made under the previous government when the Yukon Act was amended to increase the size of the council from five to seven members and to establish the Advisory Committee on Finance of three members selected by themselves from among themselves, was a first step in achieving that executive control which is necessary before any institution can be called democratic.
Our ambit'on, notwithstanding the brief that has been submitted to the Carrothers Commission by the government of Alberta, notwithstanding the suggestion of Premier Bennett of British Columbia and notwithstanding several representations made by others in this regard, is to achieve full provincial status in due course. We in the Yukon, and I know the feeling is the same in the Northwest Territories, do not wish to become any provincial backyard.
I am sure these sentiments find favour not only with the minister and his officials but with the government as well. Having said that and having recognized, as I know the minister does, that there is a rising tide of resentment in both Territories against the continuing situation whereby people living in these Territories have no direct control over the development of their respective Territories, there must be evolved now some kind of plan which will bring us to the point of autonomy in the near future.
The provisions of the British North America Act, particularly those of section 146, provide the machinery whereby provincial status can be accomplished. In the Yukon we are moving in that direction. We have had over 65 years of history in the development

DEBATES	March 3, 1966
of the institution of government and of an acquaintanceship with the machinery of that kind of government. Those in the Northwest Territories are not so fortunate.
Members of the committee will, I am sure, be aware of the fact that in the Yukon Territory the council is wholly elective, whereas in the Northwest Territories a minority of four holds elective office and an appointed five councillors hold the balance of power. I know this will be changed in the amendments to the Northwest Territories Act to be introduced during this session.
We believe that we in the Territories exist in a state of vassalage. We are ignored in all high level deliberations. It is not good enough to say with respect to the functioning of federal-provincial conferences that we can send an observer. There must be participation. Policies and projects cannot be evolved affecting the development of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories unless there is participation in the design of those policies and projects by those who live in these Territories.
All of the countries of the Commonwealth which now enjoy representative institutions and responsible government have passed through a provis;onary period. That has been our history in Canada. That has been the history of any evolution of the territorial form of government through to the state or provincial form of government. There has to be a growth of population; there has to be a certain degree of political training which will prepare emerging areas for the responsibilities of autonomy.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I draw to the attention of the minister and members of this committee, and I do so now because when amendments to the Yukon Act and the Northwest Territories Act come up for discussion-I give the minister fair notice now-it will be our object to seek certain amendments to those pieces of legislation which will, we think, ach eve the desired end of accomplishing this planned progress to autonomy in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. The Yukon was established as a separate district as far back as 1895. Well before the western provinces became provinces, the Yukon was already a separate district. In 1889, it was created a separate territory and at that time a council was set up. We have, therefore, evolving for well over 65 years a territorial form of government in which there has been participation in
March 3. 1966

legislative function, and in that function only by the citizens in the Yukon.
My proposals, very briefly set out are these, and they are what the minister can expect as amendments proposed to the Yukon Act. I propose, first, that the administration of justice be passed from federal to territorial control in the Yukon. I am not speaking now of the Northwest Territories. The Yukon has been prepared for some years now for the acceptance of this responsibility, I mean some recent years. There should be set up in the Yukon an attorney general's office with full responsibility for the administration of justice. The remarkable, and I say this without any reflection intended whatever, increase in the thousands of dollars being now paid out to crown counsel and to other officials in connection with the administration of justice in the Yukon would seem to fully justify this proposal.
From a point prior to 1962, where the average for the previous decade was $12,000 to $15,000 a year paid out for this kind of fee and expense, it has increased in the last three years to $25,000 and $35,000 per year. This amount of money will support, and easily support, the establishment and existence of an attorney general's office. It will also allow salary scales to be raised to a level where capable professional people will be attracted. The minister knows the difficulty we have been experiencing in obtaining legal counsel there in the last three years. We have not found anyone yet. The reason is simple, the salary scale is just too low.
Second, I propose that the lands administration function that is now carried out in Ottawa by the minister's department in so far as the Yukon is concerned, be transferred to Whitehorse. It seems a ridiculous situation where you have a territory comprising about 207,000 square miles, and where it takes two, three or more months to obtain title to a 50 by 100 foot building lot. This situation simply is not acceptable any longer. I know the minister will agree with me that the accelerating influx of industrial activity in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, particularly in the Yukon, demands that decisions be made on the spot. Industries that are in the Yukon to set up mining complexes want decisions of a municipal nature now. They do not want to be bogged down by an exchange of correspondence taking months between officials in Whitehorse, officials in Ottawa and themselves. This is where time is consumed.

Supply-Northern Affairs
The next step in the evolution I suggest is increasing the size of the wholly elected council from seven members to 15. I know the minister is going to consider that a rather large jump, and will want some justification for it. Probably his officials will want to test the merit of that suggestion as well. I suggest 15 because of the existence of a state of affairs now where the 7 man council has developed into nothing more nor less than a sort of permanent opposition to the administration. Everything that is proposed in council by the administration is opposed by the council, and it is because there is no division of opinion on the council; it is because there is not that division that is found in a house such as this or in a house such as exists in the democratic institutions of the provinces. You cannot have a division of opinion with seven representatives.
I believe, although it may be more or less than 15, that that kind of division of opinion can only be had if you have a sufficient number of individual representatives on the council so that you are going to have emerge a majority opinion and a minority opinion. The second reason for increasing the size of the council is to attract to the elective offices the calibre of individual which it is so desirable to have form any representative institution. People of that calibre do not wish to run, for several reasons. One of those reasons is that they do not want to have a part in constantly opposing the administration, which is the situation now and will continue to be unless either my suggestion or some equivalent is adopted.
There is another reason for increasing the size of the council. By increasing its size you will allow that kind of flexibility which will permit the extraction from it of at least five representatives from among the members of the council who will be able to accept executive responsibility. I am opposed to any retrograde step or alterations of the suggestion I am making now to increase the council whereby you would appoint members to the council or to the legislative assembly. This principle of appointment denies the very principle of the democratic institution itself. The only argument of which I am aware in support of appointing people to legislative bodies in the state of development in which the territories are now, is that they will provide the expertise necessary and which perhaps the elected members of council in the Northwest Territories, for example, do not have. This is no justification because this
2164	COMMONS
Supply-Northern Affairs expertise can be had by calling before council, as we have been doing in the Yukon for years, the necessary expert advice and testimony, including that of the very capable employees of the government from time to time. As a matter of fact, I can remember when the present member for the Northwest Territories appeared before the council to advise the council on the implementation of hospital insurance in the Yukon.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The next step would be increasing to five the size of the advisory committee, which now consists of three. These five members would be selected by the leader of the majority of the elected council of 15. In other words, you would have emerging from the 15 man elected body, a leader of the majority opinion, whether you called them red and white, Grit and Tory, or Socialist and Social Credit. You would have a split of opinion and the leader of that majority selects from it his advisory committee. There would have to be the clothing of that executive committee with executive responsibility. I do not know whether the minister is shaking his head indicating disagreement with these proposals.

This is a real problem and we discussed the question the minister has raised with several of those in the Yukon. I had anticipated this problem, as had others. But if you think for a moment, no matter how you cut the pie, with 15 members you are not going to wind up with the undesirable situation that you have in this House of Commons. Regardless of how you cut it you are always going to have a majority numerically-and I mean a numerical majority. I am sure the minister will agree with me that even though you might find within a majority group shades of opinion, particularly in the Yukon, you are going to get from 15 members that kind of opinion that is close enough among seven or eight members so as to form a majority opinion. I do not know whether I have put across that idea to the minister, but none the less that is what would happen. There simply is not that kind of probability in the Yukon, as is the case in this house.
As the minister and his officials know, we in the Yukon are now looking after education; that is administered there. The whole forestry function is carried out in the Yukon, even though it is a federal responsibility. The

DEBATES	March 3, 1966
game function is carried out there. We have the welfare function carried out in part there, though the administrative function could all be carried out there. The public works function territorially is carried out there. It is the plan to transfer the administration and the maintenance of the Alaska highway from the federal Department of Public Works to the territorial department of public works, or to highways or the engineering department, in April of 1967. So that these administrative functions are now being, or will be in the near future, carried out in Whitehorse.
It is but a short step to pass executive responsibility to the five-man nucleus of the cabinet that I suggest. At the moment, as the minister knows, the council has only one fiscal prerogative. It has only one control over the executive, and that is to refuse to pass supply. They had the same kind of power in the early days in Manitoba, in 1879, just before the district of Assiniboia became the province of Manitoba. The minister will well recall from his reading of history when Frederick Haultain led a group of dissatisfied Manitobans and refused to pass supply, and the civil service had to go out and cut wood to pay the rent and to eat.
I am not suggesting for a moment that the people of the Yukon will revolt in that fashion, but I am suggesting that the feeling in the Yukon, not only among the general population but among the employees in his own department and territorial civil servants, has now reached the stage of almost antiimperialism. Our commissioner is resigning. It is embarrassing for me to refer to him when he is sitting above me, but as I understand it, what he is saying is that he cannot drive a team of horses with reins 4,000 miles long.
Because of the role the members of the council have adopted of constantly opposing the administration, this has placed the commissioner in the position of being torn between two responsibilities. He gets static from Ottawa because he cannot keep the council in line, and he gets static from the councillors because he cannot get what they want from Ottawa. So there has to be some kind of coming together of the legislative and executive functions there.
The opponents to this kind of reform will say that he who pays the piper should call the tune.
