Perhaps the minister will bear with me a moment or two. They then advanced the second argument, that there is not sufficient population in the Yukon to justify this kind of reform. I suggest that on both counts these arguments fall to the ground.
There is precedent for the population argument, since in the province of Manitoba you had a white population less than the population today in the Yukon upon formation of the district of Assiniboia into the province of Manitoba. At that time the province of Manitoba was heavily subsidized by federal moneys, yet executive control was passed over. Even today the province of Newfoundland and the province of Prince Edward Island are heavily subsidized by federal funds. The province of Prince Edward Island has a population of 100,000 people, with four members in this house and with Senate representation. There is no Senate representation for the north at all and there is no executive responsibility.
There is the precedent of yesterday and the precedent of today for saying that the fiscal argument should not affect this decision, as well as for saying that the population should not affect the decision. Surely the test should be: Is it or is it not desirable to erect democratic institutions in that part of the country where the people are going to have a real and effective voice in their own local affairs? This is not the case in the Yukon. You can pass resolution after resolution and give opinion after opinion, but this is not the same as evolving policy. A denial of this kind of reform is simply saying to the people of the Yukon that they do not have the kind of individual who is responsible enough to look after the territorial taxpayers' dollar and the Canadian taxpayer's dollar. Yet we are giving them this kind of responsibility now particularly in the field of education. As the minister knows, there is the whole structure of the territorial civil service quite separate and distinct from the federal civil service which now exists in the Yukon and has for many years, and which performs a wholly territorial function.
We bargain for federal moneys-indeed, this is one of the reasons the advisory committee is here now

on the same basis as the provinces. We negotiate separately and sign separately the same kind of federal-provincial fiscal agreements as does any province. We pay taxes in the territory. Granted, we do not pay enough to maintain government and services, but no more so than Manitoba did when

Supply-Northern Affairs it became a province and no more so than Newfoundland and P.E.I. do today. However, there is representation from those provinces on the decision-making bodies which prepare and complete the fiscal agreements with the provinces.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
What earthly reason can there be for having no representation when these fiscal decisions are made under the federal government and the territory. Instead of that, what happened was that the federal government said, "Here is the contract; you sign it." That was the end of it. You could not say yes, no, or maybe.
It would be my suggestion, to round out these reforms that I proposed to the minister and to the committee this evening, that these executive responsibilities should be passed in the fields I have mentioned, to the enlarged executive committee. I do not suggest for a moment that water resources, oil and gas or mineral resources should leave the federal jurisdiction, no more than they left the federal jurisdiction when the western provinces were created in 1905.
A period is required during which the elected council must gain the skill of government before the important resource responsibilities pass to it. It took 25 years in the case of the western provinces. In my submission, perhaps it would take as much as three or four sessions of the new kind of assembly that I envisage in the Yukon to be ready to assume the whole resource responsibility.
I am suggesting that the term of the council be extended from the existing three years to four years. I suggest that the council be allowed to set their own indemnity. Surely if we have a representative institution that we are going to clothe with any kind of responsibility, the first kind of responsibility we must entrust to it is that of setting its own indemnities, instead of being told by this house how much they are going to get.

to me this time.
I know that the proposal will very likely be made, in the amendments to the Yukon Act to be brought before the house, that the house be asked to set the salary. Let the members of the council set it themselves. They are the ones who are going to have to accept the reaction of the electorate up there. If they set it too high they will not get back into office, and perhaps the taxpayers of the Yukon and Canada will be better off if that decision were left entirely up to the council.
I suggest, too, that the prohibition-and of course this would be a consequential sort of amendment that would follow upon the adoption of the reforms I have suggested-contained in section 24 of the Yukon Act be removed in so far as that provision affects the executive responsibilities in those departments which I have suggested should be transferred to the executive of the enlarged assembly.
Education, public works or engineering, or whatever it might be called, health and welfare, education, justice, revenue and finance, resources, except oil, gas, water and minerals, but including game, tourism, forests, would be transferred. These would pretty well take up the energies of the five man executive committee that I propose.
I urge the minister to take these very broad proposals which are alterable in the main into consideration.
Economic events of recent years in the Yukon should indicate to the minister the tremendous potential of the country itself. Problems that are arising because of this tremendous acceleration are becoming more serious as each day passes, and something has to be done. I believe the reforms I have suggested are reasonable reforms. They are not radical.
I believe that the real control of the federal government representing the taxpayer of Canada as a whole will be the fact that the federal government will retain control over the major resources responsibilities; therein lies the basic economic reality that the Yukon has to offer to the over-all national economic fabric.
When the amendments to the Yukon Act are placed before the house I would very sincerely hope to see incorporated in them the proposals I have put to the minister, or alternatives bearing very close resemblance to them.

[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
It seems as though the government wants to get rid of the residents in the park. These people have made investments there and are enjoying their stay, but they want some security. I have lived adjacent to this wilderness area and I know something about it. We have a wilderness area extending 2,000 miles north. speechtext:
I realize the committee expects everyone to be as brief as possible. I did have quite a number of things to take up while the estimates of this department were being discussed, but I will try to be brief. I want to point out one thing before I launch into my remarks. I have heard observations in the last three or four days, we heard them last night from the acting house leader and again tonight, to the effect that the government is anxious to get these estimates through. I also heard two people the other evening on the local television station, I believe Colin Parker and Mr. Tom Earle, say that if the Conservative opposition continued the filibuster the civil servants would not be paid.
I should like to say for the record at this time that if the government had handled the business of the country properly, if we had come back last September, as promised by the Prime Minister, we would have had time to scrutinize these estimates in the way the people of Canada expect us to do.
I should like to make a few comments with regard to the Roads to Resources policy. I know the minister or the chairman might say this Roads to Resources program has now been put under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. In answer to a question by the hon. member for Mackenzie, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources directed the question to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys who said, more or less, that a number of the provinces had not yet spent their allotment under this program.
Now, in the last session we were asking questions concerning the plans of the government for extending or re-establishing the
March 3, 1966

Roads to Resources program. We were told at that time the government intended to come up with a different type of program which would be much better. If the program they have evolved is the program for the Northwest Territories, if that is the one they have substituted for the Roads to Resources program, I should like to suggest to the minister it will be of no help whatever to the people in the northern parts of the provinces. These people were grateful to the previous administration for inaugurating the Roads to Resources program. The Minister without Portfolio mentioned he thought this was one of the better programs that had been introduced in the last few years. I certainly agree with him. When we do not get an answer from the government regarding any extension or re-establishment, I wonder whether the Prime Minister has probably convinced his colleagues in the cabinet that, as he said once before, this would be nothing but roads from igloo to igloo.
I do not want to keep harping on that statement of the Prime Minister, but he did make it. If we do not hear something from the government fairly soon, the people in the northern parts of the provinces will become convinced that possibly this is the attitude of the government. I hope that the minister or his colleagues in the cabinet will study this situation, because if you talk to mining people and lumbermen and people in the tourist industry, they will tell you, if it is not already realized by those on the front benches, just how much necessity there is for a continuation of this program.
I want to speak very briefly on a subject which may not seem of too much importance to the committee tonight, with everyone being in a hurry, but it relates to one aspect of northern affairs, the Canadian wildlife service. I have discussed several matters with the director, Dr. Munro, who has been very helpful. At the present time we have this huge development coming along in Manitoba, the Nelson River power project. We have recently had other power projects developed in Manitoba. I feel, as do all members in the game and fish associations as well as interested persons in Manitoba, that a very thorough look should be taken by the Canadian wildlife service at the wildlife habitat in the Nelson River area. Correspondence has passed back and forth between the minister and various game and fish associations, and the minister has advised these associations that wildlife in the provinces, and renewable

Supply-Northern Affairs resources, come within the jurisdiction of the provinces. However, I would point out that under the Migratory Birds Convention Act the federal government has a distinct responsibility.
On looking at the estimates I see that the amount of money allotted to the Canadian wildlife service is very small, which means it is not always possible to do the work they feel they would like to do. Therefore I would suggest to the minister that he take a look at this with his officials to see whether it would be possible under the migratory birds treaty for the Canadian wildlife service to send men into this area to make sure that the wildlife habitat as far as geese and other migratory birds are concerned is well protected. I would ask the minister to ensure, particularly in view of the diversion of the Churchill River into the Nelson, which might result in lower water levels, that nothing will be done to disturb to a great extent, or disturb to any extent if possible, the wildlife habitat in the area.
The wildlife service has admitted that the watershed of the Nelson River in its northern region is recognized as a great potential geese habitat, something which must be protected for the benefit of future generations. However, I am not going to spend the time tonight on this subject, although I should like to; as I said, I do realize the situation.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
I should like to spend a few minutes on some of the problems facing the Indian people, not only of the area which I represent but of northern Canada. Indian affairs, as I understand it, come under the Minister of Northern Affairs, with the new addition I believe of "Indian affairs." I know that the officials of the Indian affairs branch over the years have been spending countless hours trying to come up with some solution to the tremendous problems which face our Indian people. I do not profess to have the solution but I do feel that I have some constructive suggestions to make and I feel that the time is long past due when some of those programs should be adapted. In the area which I have the honour to represent there are 17 Indian reservations comprising some 13,000 or 14,000 people of Indian blood. They are still living on reservations. Over the last ten years that population has increased to its present figure from 7,000 to 8,000.
As the people in the Indian affairs branch realize, if something is not done about their
March 3, 1966

Supply

Northern Affairs problem soon, it is going to become much greater within the next 15, 20 or 25 years. People in the Indian affairs branch realize that something should be done, but sufficient money is not provided. I know that the director of the branch, Mr. Battle has a genuine interest in the welfare of the people, as have many of his officials. I also know that he is handicapped by insuflcient money to spend. One thing which would not cost too much money is for those people who wish to remain there-and it is my intention to see that those who wish to remain there shall do so,-to have their conditions improved as quickly as possible. If the government keeps its promises, it will improve the situation of those Indian people. We have glaring examples in my constituency-

speechtext:
I would suggest to the minister that one of the most urgent considerations is to provide Indian people with electric power. I know that this seems to be almost impossible. I can tell the minister that in the province of Manitoba the provincial agency in charge of power has the equipment on hand, is prepared to go in and do those things, and do it now. It is just a matter of getting some financial assistance from the Indian Affairs Branch. I think the minister should look at the situation to provide financial assistance as quickly as possible, because if this is not done these people are going to be without these services for many, many years.
I hear people at the far end of the house and on the government side saying, "Let us get on with the estimates." However, I can assure those hon. members that I am not standing up here for any political reason. I am standing up here and speaking for 14,000 Indian people in northern Manitoba who sent me down to speak for them. I should like, in conclusion, to say to the minister that on some reservations conditions are quite good. For instance at Island Lake, conditions may be better, because it is the location of an agency. At Island Lake they have a saw mill; they have inaugurated a net hanging project

which last year brought in between $6,000 to $10,000 in revenue for the people.
The people can do these things themselves under supervision. They instituted upgrading courses. They are very successful and in general they have a well run reservation. On some other reservations, nothing is done for them. No guidance is given to them, possibly for lack of funds. I say that improvements to these reservations could be made for very little money. Instructors must be sent in to guide these people. In more favourable circumstances these people could lead a much better life.
There is one final point I wish to make. It relates to the designated areas and I hope the minister will not say that I should be raising this subject with the Department of Industry. The area of which I have been speaking is one which I have been trying to get the minister concerned to recognize as being a designated area for two or three months. He tells me it does not meet the criteria-that the unemployment figures do not correspond with the figures which are acceptable.
I implore the minister to have his officials check with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. He will find that unemployment officers nearest the areas where these people live and where they would have to register are so far away that there are no figures whatsoever. On my way to Ottawa at the beginning of this session I ran into two people each of whom was willing to go into northern Manitoba and put up a fish processing plant costing in the neighbourhood of $200,000. They would put the plants up tomorrow if this was a designated area. Skilled labour is not necessary in this kind of work. The Indian people could do it. Each of these plants would provide work for 60 of the Indian people-they would need no more than a week's training.
I trust the minister will have his officials look into this matter as quickly as possible to see whether this area of northern Manitoba could not be declared a designated area. Whatever this might cost, the benefits would far surpass that cost.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to co-operate also with the Conservatives in stretching out the debate as much as possible so that midnight comes fast.
We are now studying supply for the Department of Northern Affairs and National
March 3, 1966

Resources. I should like to know if the imbroglio between Ottawa and Quebec, with regard to the Quebec Eskimos, has been settled; if the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) has complied with the requests, made time and time again, by hon. Rene Levesque, that Quebec be given jurisdiction over the Eskimos in Northern Quebec? We should like the minister to tell us who has jurisdiction over Eskimo affairs in that part of Canada, namely in Northern Quebec.
A lot has been said about national parks these past few hours. Under that item, the department will spend this year $13,551,000. A number of national parks are listed from all parts of western and eastern Canada: Banff, Elk, Jasper, Kootenay, Revelstoke and Glacier; Prince Albert, Mount Riding, Wat-erton Lakes, Yoho. But there is hardly any mention of expenditures for another park, although it does come under jurisdiction of the federal government, I mean the Gatineau park in the Ottawa area.
I appreciate the fact that the department has already spent large amounts on the development of Gatineau park to accommodate tourists, but there are in the Gatineau, as most hon. members who have visited the area know, unlimited possibilities.
The population of the Ottawa-Hull area is almost as large as the population of Saskatchewan, that of Alberta or of the Maritime provinces taken together. This park contains beautiful lakes which should get more attention from federal authorities. I point out to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources that his department should pay more attention to the Gatineau park and develop more facilities there for tourists who come not only from Ottawa and the area, from eastern and western Canada, but also from the United States.
If the department can spend $13.5 million on national parks, it seems to me it would be possible to take part of that amount or increase it, if the minister decides to do so and the cabinet agrees, in order to improve the Gatineau park.
In another field, the minister is doubtless aware of a plan put forward by a Sudbury engineer, Mr. Kierans. This engineer established a realistic plan to feed the great lakes from James Bay, Hudson Bay and the Arctic Ocean through the Harricanaw river crossing Chapleau riding and part of Villeneuve riding, to raise the levels of the great lakes. This is a vast project involving hundreds of millions of dollars, but the minister surely knows
Supply-Northern Affairs that the United States has to raise the level of lake Michigan for instance, on the shores of which stands the great city of Chicago.
It would certainly be to Canada's advantage to make a thorough study of the project conceived by Mr. Kierans, the engineer, which, if it were carried out, would provide for a wonderful development all along the Harricanaw river and even along James Bay, into which this river empties. Then, it seems to me, Canada could export that water to the great lakes and the United States, while helping those Canadian cities which, at the present time, are complaining about the fact the water level of the great lakes is getting lower and lower each year.
Mr. Chairman, those were the few remarks I had to make and I hope that item 1 will be passed right away.

Mr. Chairman, I will be very brief. This arises out of a statement made by the minister the day before yesterday, which appears in a sentence on the right hand column at page 1948 of Hansard. This is a part of what he said:
... I shall later, but I thought it was an unusual brief because I find that with respect to the total park space in the provinces, combined federal and provincial parks, the province of Alberta is in third position because it has not provided provincial parks to any degree whatsoever.
Mr. Chairman, that statement is not only wrong, it is unfair and a callous and arrogant disregard for the viewpoint of the administration of the province of Alberta. The minister knows very well that all the Rocky Mountain area along the continental divide in Alberta is national park area, except for a very small piece in the Crowsnest Pass. How in the name of common sense can we have provincial parks where there already are federal parks? That statement is wrong because there is more national park area in the province of Alberta than in all the rest of Canada put together. I intended to get the exact figure, but I think there are more than 60 provincial parks in Alberta. There are five provincial parks in my own riding and that is not unusual in respect of other ridings. That same pattern is followed from the United States border to well north of Edmonton.
Mr. Chairman, the minister's statement is one of the most unfair and incorrect that have been made in this house. Let me suggest to him that this is not the kind of attitude the government and the people of Alberta expect
March 3, 1966

Supply-Northern Affairs from federal cabinet ministers, if there is going to be any kind of co-operation in evolving policies in respect of national parks which will be satisfactory to the people of Alberta.
I could say a great deal more on this subject but I will leave my remarks at that, because of the pressure of time.

Mr. Chairman, before vote 15 is carried I should like to put a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. My question deals with historic sites. In order that the minister will realize the significance of the question I wish to review briefly to my correspondence with the department. While my question is directed to the minister and, as I have said, concerns historic sites, I would point out that the correspondence dates back to August 21, 1963, and was directed at that time to Mr. W. F. Whitman, General Manager of the Real Estate Branch, Department of Transport. At that date I inquired as to the future usage of the lighthouse site at Point Clarke in the county of Bruce. On September 3, 1963, my letter was acknowledged and I was provided with this information:
The lightstation has now been converted to an automatic light thus making the lightkeeper's dwelling and the 2.13 acres of land and land covered by water forming the site, surplus to departmental requirements.
A number of people have shown interest in acquiring this property as well as the National Historic Sites Division of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and no action will be taken towards the disposal of this property until we hear from that department as to whether or not this site is required as a national historic site.
The letter closes by saying:
Should it develop that this land is not required as an historic site, then in keeping with departmental policy, as a number of parties have shown interest in the property, we will arrange to have it advertised for sale by public tender.
That letter is signed by the minister of the department, George J. Mcllraith. In November of 1963 I made representation on behalf of the Bruce County Historical Association to learn what had happened with regard to the possibility of this property being put up for sale and disposed of, being
March 3, 1966

aware of the fact that the department thought it could possibly be acquired as an historic site. This representation was acknowledged on December 10, 1963. At that time I inquired into this matter on behalf of the society and was provided with information concerning the structure of the lighthouse. To show the significance of this historic site I wish to quote this paragraph:
Unfortunately no plans or detailed descriptions are available since the structure was erected in 1859. However, we are able to inform you that it has a masonry exterior and is 35' x 22' x 12' high to the eaves.
On August 13, 1964, I again inquired of the minister what decision had been reached relative to the disposal of the department's holding at Point Clarke. On August 18 my correspondence was acknowledged and the minister stated:
As previously mentioned to you, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has indicated an interest in this property for a national historic site, and I am now informed that we are still awaiting a reply from that department before a decision can be reached. You may rest assured that we will keep you posted on any future developments.
On September 30, 1964, in answer to a question which I placed on the order paper I received this reply:
The Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada has been asked to study this matter at its next meeting to be held this October. After the Board has presented its recommendations on the historical and architectural significance of the Point Clarke lighthouse, the minister will be in a position to reach the decision.
That was September 30, 1964, and I still have not received the decision.
On February 17, 1965, I placed this question on the order paper:
Did the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources arrive at a decision regarding the acquisition of the Point Clarke light site for a national historic site when the historic sites and monuments board met in October?
The minister replied as follows:
The historic sites and monuments board of Canada have not made any recommendations with respect to the Point Clarke light site.
Since we are now into 1966, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister once again if a decision will soon be handed down?

There are two comments I have to make under this item, one of which is related to general policy of the present government in relation to national parks. I just fail to understand the arrogance and determination-there are no other words to use-of
Supply-Northern Affairs the government to impose upon the people who live in these parks a policy which does not make sense, rhyme or reason to me as well as a lot of other people. The type of answer we have had here tonight, is indicative of this. The only thing we can say is that the minister is determined to completely end the existence of his party in the province of Alberta, because this is exactly what is going to take place. It is not just those who belong to the political party to which I belong, but the members of his own party and the citizens of the province of Alberta as a whole, who feel this way. The claim of the administration that they are retaining the wilderness of Canada for the good of the citizens of Canada is something we all accept and recognize as being correct.
But the park area should be developed in a logical way not only for wilderness beauty, and to deny such development is something that does not make sense. All of us who know Switzerland realize that the beauty of Switzerland has been enhanced by the development that has taken place in that country. As long as we have the natural beauty that we have in our own lofty mountain areas, anything less than the development of all aspects of them would be sheer folly. To separate, shall I say, the sport of skiing and other seasonal sports that quite logically fits within the natural setting of the mountainous area we have, is to deny the recreational facilities that are second to none in the entire world.
The attitude in regard to the proposed establishment of the winter Olympics in 1972 is indicative of a shortsighted, narrow minded policy. There is the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway going through Banff national park and the Canadian National going through Jasper. There is No. 1 highway going up the centre of Banff park and also an important highway going through Jasper. There is no reason why there cannot be an area on both sides of the highway and railroad reserved for commercial development, thus giving the people who live within the townsites confidence that we will adopt a system which will allow those who live in the area to serve the tourists and other essential services.
There is no reason why facilities cannot be developed for recreation in the summer and recreation in the winter. There is no reason why the hundreds of square miles of wilderness cannot be preserved in its natural beauty for other types of recreation that attracts
March 3, 1366

Supply-Northern Affairs so many tourists to the area. It seems to me that any logical park policy has to be adapted to three purposes, so far as the Rocky Mountain parks are concerned. First of all, the rights of the citizens who live within the park to service the facilities within the park, cannot be denied. These Canadian citizens earn a living that way. They are not just a lot of promoters and money makers either. They are Canadian citizens with just as much right to make a living in this part of Canada as anybody in any other part of the country. So let us be logical and give them an area where the commercial development which is required in parks can be situated. Let us provide facilities for sport and general recreation which is required by the Canadian people, and at the same time let us preserve the natural beauty of our wilderness areas. We not only can provide the type of recreation and sport facilities and essential business operations which are necessary, but we can enhance the beauty of our parks as well if we act properly.
[DOT] (11:00 p.m.)
I will be saying more about this in the estimates for next year, but I do want to bring to the attention of the minister just one example of administrative inefficiency which does take place sometimes in our parks. Rather than speak on the matter myself I should like to quote a letter which condenses the particular problem much more adequately than I could express it. It is written by the pilot of aircraft CF-NTS who, on February 26, had occasion to fly into the Banff townsite expecting to land at the airstrip there which is adjacent to the town, bringing with him certain personages on a charter flight. He says:
Before making the flight I checked with the Department of Transport and they were unable to give me any information as to the runway and its condition. I then placed a telephone call to the Parks Department number given to me by the Department of Transport and there was no answer, so I then telephoned the R.C.M. Police in Banff, and they informed me that the strip was plowed, but only to a width of 45 feet and 1500 feet long. I, therefore, took off on this flight with three passengers on board, and before landing I flew down low over the strip and from my observation it looked safe to land. Upon landing I found that the strip had only been plowed to approximately 20 feet, and that on the right hand side of the strip there was a ridge of snow approximately 3 feet high. I further wish to state that at the end of the supposedly plowed runway, there was an airplane stuck in the snow, and that evening some seven of us pushed It out and it was taxied into a little small alcove near the trees. At this time I observed approximately half of the runway had been plowed, and the other half just
[Mr. Thompson.!
partially plowed. I deemed this strip so dangerous that 1 had my passengers get a U-Drive and drive into Calgary. I was lucky enough by the grace of God to get off this strip by myself after dropping my three passengers, their baggage, and everything in the airplane that could be taken loose.
Is this the kind of service which is rendered by our national parks in servicing an essential airstrip, essential both at this time of the year as well as in summer. It seems to me that something better than this should be given those who wish to use this type of facility, certainly better than appears to be the case here. I trust that the minister will investigate this matter and see that something similar does not happen again.

speechtext:
As all members of the committee realize, this particular item appears in an unusual position. It is listed under the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Perhaps for that very reason it should not go unnoticed. Though I do not intend to speak at any length on this matter, let me say that this administrative change to another area of the operations of the federal government may in the long run prove to have been a valuable move.
One of the results would be that the whole situation in respect of the Indian people in the country will receive an increased measure of attention in line with what I think has been a dream not only on the part of the government but on the part of parliament. I would have liked to make several speeches on this particular question; but tonight I wish to deal only with one which, in my view, raises some of the more fundamental issues with regard to the Indian people in Canada, and that is whether we of European ancestry are going to be able to hold up our heads before them.
This question, so far as I am concerned, relates to what is going to happen on a matter that was the subject which brought about the introduction of several bills in the recent period of parliamentary activity. On December 14, 1963 the then Minister of Citizenship and Immigration introduced Bill C-130, An Act to provide for the Disposition of Indian claims. As members of the committee will recall this bill had its genesis in the joint committee on Indian affairs which brought out a report in 1961; but Bill C-130 after a preliminary stage in the house, was circulated widely throughout the country, and then on June 21, 1965 we had a successor bill, Bill C-123, which was to have been referred for consideration last fall to a special committee for detailed consideration.
At this time arrangements were under way for the appearance of Indian people and others before that committee, until the bill, along with a number of other things, came to an untimely end with the dissolution of parliament. I might also draw the attention of
[Mr. Laing.J
the committee again to the fact that in addition to the bills introduced on the government side, to which I have referred, there was in 1963 Bill C-67, entitled An Act Respecting the Canada Court of Indians Claims, introduced by my colleague the hon. member for Skeena. When we left here last fall for the recess, those of us who had been following this matter fully expected that this would be immediately the subject of a great deal of discussion and consideration in the special committee. We hoped that out of that would come changes in the bill, as it was introduced, in line with the thinking of the Indian people which would bring us near to what might be termed a complete solution of the ancient wrongs that were done to the Indian people, so far as it was humanly possible that it be done.	_
As we all know that bill died. Now, I would like to refresh the minister's attention and refer to a question which the member for Skeena asked him on February 14. This is found on page 1157 of Hansard. The hon. member said:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. When may we expect the introduction in the house of a bill regarding the Indian claims commission? When the minister answers that question perhaps he might also indicate whether that bill has been delayed up to now by revision of any previous bill.
The minister will recall that he replied in these terms:
Mr. Speaker, the delay that has eventuated has had more than one cause. It has come from the quarters with which my hon. friend and myself are familiar, namely, the province of British Columbia, where the Indian people seem to prefer to take a concentrated second look before proceeding.
[DOT] (11:20 p.m.)
Some Indians of British Columbia indicated they would prefer to consider their particular position in negotiation prior to introduction of the bill. I have told the legal adviser of the Indians in the province of British Columbia that I am prepared to discuss with them this subject, and I have had a preliminary meeting with him, before any action is taken.
Mr. Chairman, I think the answer the minister gave to the house on February 14 re-opened this whole matter in several very important respects. It particularly re-opened the question as far as the Indian people of British Columbia are concerned, but it also leaves unanswered what the minister may have in mind as far as the Indian people in the rest of Canada are concerned in relation to the proposals that were put forward in the
March 3. 1986	COMMONS
.government bill that went down the drain when parliament was dissolved.
I realize that the minister was limited because this question was asked on orders of the day, but I think it is important, now that we have the estimates of the Indian affairs branch before us, for the minister to take this opportunity to expand somewhat on the brief preliminary statement he made in answer to that question which itself raised some very important and fundamental questions as to what he has in mind. I hope the minister will give a somewhat expanded statement and that it will be one which will be, shall I say, encouraging as far as I am concerned.
I might just remind the minister before he replies that some of us recall an attempt made in 1927 to settle this whole Indian question by a special Indian grant of $100,000 per year in lieu of treaty money, as it is often described, to the Indians of British Columbia.
I mention that fact because I am hopeful that when the minister talks about negotiating with the Indian people of British Columbia in respect of the Indian land question and its settlement, in a broader context than was set out in the Indian claims bill, he is not thinking in terms of the kind of settlement that was made in 1927.

The year 1967 is the centennial of confederation, but that is a mere incident in the long history of the Indian people of this country. Let us, who are the inheritors of this great nation, plan now to assure that the year 1967 will be the year in which the ancient rights of the Indian people will be safeguarded and extended so that the Indian people can be given new opportunities and take new pride in this their native land.

I notice that under the grants item the cash payments to Indians have risen considerably. I remember the remarks of the hon. member of a few years ago, the late Mr. Hardie, when speaking of the hardship that was worked on the Indians and the very small amount of money being paid to them in many parts of the country. If the grants were doubled, tripled or made even higher than that these people could still not afford to maintain a decent standard of living.
We have a responsibility, as the hon. member for Carleton has said, to solve these problems that have been facing us for a long time. I believe there is general agreement that there will not be much difficulty in establishing the Indian Claims Commission. During the election campaign I heard many candidates speaking of this commission as though it were an established fact and I heard many government members indicating that this was already part of the status quo. If this is true, I suppose there really is no objection to it. But we are interested in this question, and if the minister does not want to give us the information now perhaps he would send it to me. I should like to know the details of the agreement that has been worked out with the province of Ontario to solve the problem that has arisen in parts of that province and which has resulted in a change in the method of handling welfare payments.
The reason for my concern is not that the Indian will not be better off under the Ontario welfare scheme than he was under the federal government scheme, because I think it is a fact that he will be better off. He will probably be twice or three times as well off under the provincial scheme. But I believe
March 3. 1966

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration we should not slough off all the problems that arise in relation to our Indians by thinking that integration can cure them. Integration is not what the Indian wants. Many Indian people have now received enough education to know they have a heritage that should be protected. Hon. members will have noticed from some of the magazine articles written recently about Indians that the Indians themselves are now doing something about their problems. This attitude has not been very apparent for many years.
If the federal government gives up responsibility in this whole field, it seems to me that while it may produce a financial gain at this time, in the end it will probably eliminate the ethnic background of the Indian peoples by reason of their integration. I do not believe that is in our interest or in the interest of the Indian. It is all well and good to have claims settled in regard to treaties that existed and were signed many years ago, although these claims should have been settled a long time ago; but there are other parts of the country where the Indians did not have signed treaties and no formal arrangement was made. In this field the federal government must maintain some type of support for the Indian.
I should also like to hear from the minister about the negotiations with the province of Quebec with regard to the Indian situation in that province. I should like to know what has been done in Quebec and, again, what is the over-all intention of the government with regard to the question of Indian problems and Indian claims.

They supported all the progressive proposals that were put forward. They also put forward a number themselves. They led us to believe that if only they could get over on the other side of the house we would get all this progressive labour legislation. They promised it in the election campaign of 1963, and of course they did not have to work very hard to put those promises together because they had had them ready since 1919.
In the first session of the last parliament, which was the first session after this government came into office, we were assured that early action would be taken on all the elements of a labour standards code; also of a labour safety code; that there would be legislation amending the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act to bring employees who come under that legislation under the same protection provided under the other labour legislation; that there would be a revamping of the Unemployment Insurance Act; and that there would be a study in depth and the consequent amendments of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.

time the provisions of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code were to begin.

The previous minister was categorical in his promise that a way would be found to make sure that the protection afforded in the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act would be the same as that provided in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, and that it would be effective on the same date. A question is on the order paper asking the ministry to provide the names of industries which have asked for deferment. That has not yet been answered.
Someone took the trouble to help me go through the Canada Gazette. Almost every major organization, such as the C.B.C., railways, trucking firms, air lines, and so on have asked for deferment with respect to section 11, which deals with the minimum $1.25 wage. This can go on for 18 months, and the minister can then give to those industries a deferment for another 18 months.
There is no reason in the world why the Department of Labour should not by now make up its mind, and why the minister should not make up his mind with respect to the applications listed in the numerous sheets of the Canada Gazette for deferment. There is no purpose to having a statute on the statute books if it is not being applied.
As I say, as I looked through the Gazette there were literally hundreds and hundreds of names of firms, who were simply asking that the minister should let them stand. There is no point in having a statute on the statute books, when in fact it is not being applied except in situations where employees have already won these things through collective bargaining and agreement. As I looked through the list of, literally, hundreds and hundreds of firms under various headings I was astounded that the minister should let this stand. He has made decisions in the case of flour and feed mills, if I remember correctly; in the case of grain elevators and so on-decisions on deferment of wage increases which I am sure he reached after careful consideration. I am not criticizing those decisions. But he has not made decisions involving highway transport, shipping firms, longshoremen, stevedores or the trucking firms in every province which have asked for one deferment or another, mainly of hours. In my submission the strike of trucking employees in this province might either not have taken place or would be greatly shortened had the minister made up his mind about the applications for deferments.

I should also state that in matters of labour and manpower there was a great disappointment concerning the labour department, in respect of unemployment insurance for fulltime farm workers and increased training allowances. It is significant to note that not a single new project has been brought up. This is the reason we will follow the activities of the new manpower department with great interest and expectation. If nothing new comes up, it would appear that this government figures that all is well on the labour front. Let us take another look.
We hope that the government will not make the mistake which it made in the late 1940's and early 1950's in not relying on the unemployment commission funds for the onslaught of a recession. Now is the time to set up the projects and crash programs to see us through as difficult a period as we will have to face probably after the centennial year.
The government knows very well that when the Conservatives came in in 1957 they were left with run-down conditions, a sick economy, and a deficit trade balance. It was left to the Conservatives to pick up the pieces, and get the country going again with progressive legislation and programs. The previous government did not seem to have a worry in the world because of the unemployment insurance commission's funds. In next to no time the cupboard was bare, because the whole country was made to suffer while the savings effect of new legislation was able to bear fruit.
It is significant to point out that the only working plans which we have today came out of that era, and still remain as progressive as the day they were born under Conservative management. I refer, first to AR.DA, second to the winter works programs, and third, to technical training assistance through vocational schools. These are the types of projects

that the present government must set up now to keep our labour force moving.
What have we had for labour since 1963 except efforts to keep these plans alive? Nothing new. As a matter of fact the slowness which has been shown in forwarding payments for winter works projects very often has created problems for our smaller communities which have been prevented from undertaking new work in the summer season because their credit was blocked at the bank for failure to pay commitments on time. Might we suggest that this be avoided in the future by faster procedures.
The $500 building bonus we will not even mention, because this government more than washed it way by imposing an 11 per cent tax on building materials, which it still stubbornly refuses to remove; and I am sure the electors will remember a long time the fact that government members voted against our amendment on this subject. We suggest that the government consider our recommendation to the effect that they make city and school taxes deductible from taxable income up to $500, as a direct assistance to the home owner and wage earner.

I should like to quote from the C.N.A. Review dated February 19, 1966 as follows; under the heading "Lost to Canada"
What is the cost to Canada of the so-called 'brain drain'? Figures newly made available by United States authorities provide some indication.
They show that in the two-year period June, 1963, to June, 1965, more than 100,000 Canadians emigrated to the U.S. Over half of these-50,709 out of 101,149-were wage or salary earners who entered the U.S. labour force.
Among them were 1,765 engineers and scientists, 1,187 technicians, 163 industrial designers, 258 university professors, 820 physicians and surgeons, 725 accountants and auditors, 2,040 trained nurses and 2,610 managers, officials and proprietors.
An underpopulated but growing country such as Canada can ill afford to lose its best educated and most highly skilled people at such a rate. We can't prevent them going, but we can improve the incentives to stay by appropriate changes in personal income tax rates, changes which would allow individuals in the middle-income groups to retain a larger share of their earnings than at present.
Do not cut me off yet. The last paragraph states:
Such action has to come sooner or later and as can be seen there are compelling reasons why it should be sooner. Your move, Mr. Sharp.
I would add to that, incentives yes, but manpower policies too; trade crusades as well to keep our labour force abreast of changing times.
Your attention is called to the province of Quebec particularly where almost 50 per cent of our unemployed are located-75,000 out of 171,000 in November, 1965. You know as well as I that after the building rush for the Expo year is over we will be in deep trouble. So again I say now is the time to prepare for this situation.
Finally, a human note on the application of unemployment insurance policies. Most of the people who are unemployed know nothing about the law and very often make innocent incomplete statements which deprive them of their benefits. Many lawyers, and I might add, many M.P.'s who are lawyers, are doing quite well in interpreting the law for them at a cost, without, however, batting one thousand as far as setting the victims straight and as far as obtaining benefits is concerned. connection. I know that he has now as a colleague, a former president of the C.N.T.U. who must have kept some of the convictions he had then. It is not merely a matter of union recognition. Indeed, I feel that the problem goes deeper than that.
If we do not take the opportunity afforded by the Department of Labour estimates, in spite of the time, it will be very difficult to obtain information on this matter. Some people promote the idea of a single labour union for the whole of Canada, including C.B.C. employees, C.N.R. workers and crown corporations workers. On the other hand, a large number of Quebec workers would prefer the C.N.T.U.
I want to uphold the cause of the workers who want to join C.N.T.U. I know that the future minister of Manpower, if he wanted to, could be a better spokesman than I. He has more experience than I have in this field and I know that he is quite familiar with the administration of the C.N.T.U. Even if he is a cabinet member, he should clearly state his position in this regard.
This is not only a fight between two unions. There is more than that. A large group of Quebec workers want to be represented by the C.N.T.U. rather than by an international union.
There is also the principle of the freedom of association. Some fought a long time-and they will know what I mean-to see that right recognized. The first right is that the worker must have the right to choose freely the association he wants to belong to.

speechtext:
On
Monday I raised a question concerning layoffs of Ford workers in Windsor. The minister replied he was looking into the matter, that he recognized the urgency of the situation and would inquire into it and answer on the following day. This, he did, and I should like to express my appreciation to him for having looked into the matter so quickly. However, the lay-offs are to begin tomorrow and this is why it is important to have an answer from the minister or from his parliamentary secretary tonight-so that we, and the workers in particular, may know how they stand in terms of these lay-offs and what success has attended the representations made by the minister on their behalf.
I think the importance of this matter goes beyond the case of these specific workers in the Ford Motor Company now threatened by lay-offs. It is important to find out the attitude of the government in relation to the Canada-U.S. agreement on automobiles. We in this party have not objected too violently to the program outlined by the Minister of Industry because we considered there was some merit in the proposals of the organized industry. Our chief concern has been the attitude which the Departments of Industry, Manpower and Labour would take when dislocation of employment became imminent.
It is important that a statement be made at this time not only in terms of what success the minister has had in his representations to the Ford Motor Company but also as an indication of what he intends to do in the future as these problems arise. A brief from union local 200 U.A.W. points out that Canadian tool work is being replaced by United States tool work and that almost 95 per cent of the tools and dies used are coming in from the United States, though we have sufficient workers and industrial facilities to produce them here in Canada.
This raises a larger problem. The automobile companies are already doing much of their research in the United States, as is perhaps understandable. But if they begin doing all their tool work in the United States and leave Canadian workers merely slapping fenders on cars when they go by on an assembly line, this has serious implications
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion for Canada. We shall become primarily assemblers and many of our most skilled and talented people will be drawn off to the United States unless a policy decision is made.
I think it is important we should know there will be employment opportunities for young Canadians when they graduate from our schools and that our schools will not be used as training grounds to provide the United States with skilled tool and die workers because there are no opportunities in this country.
I appreciate the urgency with which the minister has approached this question and I hope a statement will be forthcoming tonight which would indicate he intends to make a serious effort to speak boldly to the automobile companies. When I asked the minister whether he could give the house an assurance that no lay-offs would take place while we were negotiating, he apologized and said he had no authority to give such an assurance.
If the minister does not possess this authority, I think he had better get the authority, because fundamentally we have to make a decision in respect of whether the minister is going to make this kind of determination about our labour force, about protecting our labour force and securing jobs for our labour force, or whether the Ford Motor Company is going to make it. I would prefer to see the minister make it on behalf of the Canadian people.

We sent two representatives, one from the Department of Industry and one from the Department of Manpower, to meet with the parties, make inquiries, and try to find a solution. Today I have received a brief report stating that those two persons will be able to make a preliminary report on the whole situation tomorrow. That is the information I received today.
On the other hand, I know that 15 men are supposed to be laid oil tomorrow. That is the situation as I know it tonight. Now, when the hon. member said I should find the authority to intervene, I would like to know what kind of authority he has in mind. I know of no law that will authorize me to compel the Ford Motor Company of Canada to keep those men.
Of course we can intervene and we can exercise moral pressure on the Ford Motor Company of Canada. This is what we are trying to do. How successful we will be, we will see tomorrow. In this particular case, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a statement. I think in those cases it is unjustifiable that an enterprise or union refuse to co-operate in order to avoid company lay-offs or the opportunity to look ahead so that an attempt can be made to place those men or arrange some settlement.
[DOT] (12:30 a.m.)
In this case I am not sure that the Ford Motor Company of Canada has co-operated with the union in order to solve this problem properly. Of course I must proceed with the instruments I have in my hands, just as the unions must proceed with the instruments they have in their hands, and that is why we must wait for the report of those two men. I hope I will have it tomorrow. If we can take some action I will be very happy to take it.

(ii)	all amounts reimbursed by employers, and
